Fulham: Football League Second Division

Man City: Football League First Division

He would go on to manage England, for whom he had scored 21 goals in 63 games as a player, between February 1999 and October 2000 - resigning minutes after a 1-0 defeat to Germany in the last game played at the old Wembley Stadium.

Image: Kevin Keegan celebrates scoring against Scotland at Wembley in 1979

His time as national boss also saw England fail to get out of the group stage at Euro 2000, despite a 1-0 win over Germany, as defeats by Portugal and Romania piled on the pressure even before that defeat at the hands of Dietmar Hamann's free-kick four months later in the first qualifier for the 2002 World Cup.

A spell at Manchester City followed, which included promotion to the Premier League in 2002 as Division One champions, but Keegan left the club in March 2005, initially announcing his retirement from football.

Keegan made an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008, but only lasted eight months following tensions with the board and owner Mike Ashley.

Newcastle's statement in full on Keegan's passing

"We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply-loved figures in our club's history.

"Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

"As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James' Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

"Above all that, Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the north east with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions.

"Kevin's impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.

"At this profoundly sad time, we send our love and deepest sympathy to Kevin's wife Jean, his family, friends and all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him.

"Today, we mourn the loss of a true giant of our history, and at the appropriate moment, we will carefully consider how we shape a lasting tribute to Kevin's remarkable life and legacy. Rest in Peace, King Kev."

'Giant of the game' - Tributes come in for Keegan

Alan Shearer: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss."

Jamie Carragher: "RIP Kevin Keegan. One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies & goals galore, double Ballon D'or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game. One of the most important men in making Liverpool what it is today."

Liverpool FC: "We are deeply saddened by the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan and mourn his loss. His indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on. Rest in peace, Kevin."

England national team: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away. Kevin earned 63 international caps and scored 21 goals between 1972 and 1982, before managing the Three Lions from 1999 to 2000. Our thoughts and condolences are with Kevin's family, friends and former clubs."

Southampton FC: "We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan.

"Kevin signed for the club in 1980 as the holder of the Ballon d'Or and brought great joy to fans at The Dell and across the football world. Our thoughts are with his family and friends at this difficult time."

Manchester City FC: "Everyone at Manchester City is devastated to learn our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away, aged 75.

"Kevin was a transformative manager who brought optimism and vibrancy to City during his four-year spell in charge.

"The promotion campaign in 2001/02 will never be forgotten, and Kevin then established us once again as a top Premier League side in the years that followed. Our thoughts are with Kevin's family and friends at this very difficult time."

The English Football League: "The EFL is saddened to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan. A legend of the English game, Keegan will be remembered by generations of football fans for his impact as a player and manager. Our thoughts are with his family and friends."

Manchester United: "We are profoundly saddened by the loss of Kevin Keegan. A giant of English football, he was a cherished figure at the very highest levels of the game. Our condolences go to Kevin's family, loved ones and all those he inspired as a manager, player and person, on and off the pitch. Rest in peace, Kevin."

Former Liverpool striker David Fairclough: "Stunned. Such sad news Kevin Keegan has passed away. Absolutely devastated to hear such awful news. So many incredible memories of KK, I'm so lucky to have spent time and shared moments that have and will last a lifetime. Heartfelt condolences and love to Jean and family X. YNWA."

Sports.title: Rohit shrugs off retirement chat as he plans to play on through the 'noise'
Sports.content:
India great Rohit Sharma has shrugged off talk about his international future after scoring a century against England in the ODI series decider at Lord's.

Rumours emerged during India's defeat in the second ODI at Cardiff on Thursday that the 39-year-old could be close to retirement with the Lord's fixture a possible farewell, although that was then denied by BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia.

Rohit went on to score 138 versus England, his 34th ODI hundred, but could not prevent India from slipping to a 2-1 series defeat, hot on the heels of a 4-0 T20 drubbing.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports pundit Ravi Shastri says Rohit 'shut everyone up' with his century against England after rumours of him being phased out of the ODI side

Speaking to bcci.tv after the game, Rohit said: "Look, my job is with the bat. Come and play, represent my country, represent the team. That's what I've been told to do since I made my debut so that's what I'm going to do.

"The noise since I made my debut was there and till the time I'm going to stay here, it's always going to be there, so it doesn't really matter too much.

"What matters is what I do on the field: try and contribute to the success of the team. That's all my focus is right now. And let the noise be there. If there's no noise, there's no fun. My job is inside, their job is outside. That's how I look at it."

India captain Shubman Gill said after the final ODI that there had been no indication from Rohit that he was set to end an ODI career that has seen him amass nearly 12,000 runs across 288 matches, including three double centuries.

Image: Rohit's Lords hundred featured 17 fours and five sixes

Gill told reporters: "He has not told us anything. I think it is all out in the media. But there's not been any discussion like that in the team."

The 2027 50-over World Cup would seem the perfect stage for Rohit, who turns 40 in April, to end his career, although that decision could be taken out of his hands by selectors.

The right-hander, who quit T20 international cricket in 2024 and retired from the Test arena a year later, registered scores of 11 and 26 against England prior to his Lord's ton.

Sports.title: Guardiola holds talks over Italy head coach role
Sports.content:
The Italian Football Federation (FIGC) has met with Pep Guardiola to convince him to take over as national team head coach, according to Sky in Italy.

Paolo Maldini, the new technical director of the FIGC, and Leonardo, his advisor, travelled to Barcelona to speak with the former Man City boss.

It remains to be seen if Guardiola wants the job, but the FIGC is making concrete attempts to bring him in as the national boss.

Other candidates for the role are Roberto Mancini and Andrea Pirlo.

Maldini and Leonardo spoke with Guardiola over three days, explaining their project for the Italian national team.

The FIGC brought in Maldini and Leonardo as part of a huge shake-up in Italian football following their failure to qualify for a third consecutive World Cup.

Their task was to find a successor to Gennaro Gattuso, who left his role after missing out on qualification for this summer's tournament in North America.

Guardiola is a free agent for the first time in a decade after ending his 10-year association with Manchester City. He won 20 trophies during his time at the club and finished with a win ratio of 70.8 per cent.

Italy have failed to qualify for the last three major tournaments since winning the European Championships in 2021 under Mancini.

What Guardiola said on his future after City departure

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at the best moments from Pep Guardiola's press conference after the Spaniard confirmed he would leave Man City

Speaking to Sky Sports a year before leaving the Etihad, Guardiola revealed he would be taking a break from football when the time came for his tenure at City to end.

Following the official announcement of his departure, Guardiola doubled down on this suggestion by saying that a desire to spend more time with his family was the catalyst for his decision.

"No plans for [coaching] for a while. Otherwise I would be here. I need to step back. I will not [coach] for a while," he said during his final Manchester City press conference.

"I feel I will not have the energy every day, with expectations to fight for the title. I know myself, I have that energy, but I feel like I will not have it [in the future]."

Speaking exclusively with Sky Sports, he added: "There are things that I have not done that I want to do. I still have my father alive. I want to spend more time with him. My kids... And a lot of things as a human being I can do. I'm fortunate I can decide, that's why I took this decision."

What about England?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jack Gaughan looks at what the future may hold for Pep Guardiola following his Manchester City departure and suggests that a future role within the England national team shouldn't be ruled out

It was widely reported in 2024 that Guardiola had reached a verbal agreement with the FA to replace Gareth Southgate as the new England boss. However, he had a change of heart and opted to stay in Manchester, as Thomas Tuchel was eventually appointed, guiding England to their best World Cup finish on foreign soil.

Tuchel is contracted until the end of Euro 2028 and has vowed to see out his new deal, which was extended in February.

What is known is that Guardiola would be interested in the challenge of moving into international management. In an interview with chef Dani Garcia in 2024, he said: "What I'm not going to do is leave Manchester City and go to another country to do the same thing as I am now.

"I wouldn't have the energy to do so. I'm still here doing what I am today. But the thought of starting somewhere else, with all the process of the training and so on... no, no, no! Maybe a national team, but that's different."

Is international management the meeting in the middle for Guardiola?

Sky Sports' Callum Bishop:

Pep Guardiola is the biggest commodity in football management. That's the case now, and that was the case when he took a break after managing Barcelona. That was followed by a move to Bayern Munich, but, as Guardiola is quick to say, he is older, lacks the energy and has too much love for Manchester City to jump into a similar job.

He has expressed an interest in spending more time with his family and resting. But we know what football obsessives are like. It doesn't take long for them to get the itch back, and Guardiola is certainly a football obsessive.

A role in international management could be enough to scratch both itches. On one hand, Guardiola wouldn't be on the training pitch day in, day out, allowing him to have the time with loved ones he desires.

However, every couple of months he could work with a group of players and teach them the Guardiola way across a Euros or World Cup cycle. Not to mention that he would be entering uncharted territory.

Having already achieved everything in club football, the switch to the international game may be incredibly appealing as it is, let alone with the improved work-life balance it offers.

Imagine if he could become the first foreign manager to guide a team to World Cup glory? It sounds far-fetched considering where Italy are right now, but if anyone can do it, it's Pep.

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan, Liverpool legend and former Newcastle manager, dies aged 75
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan, the former England and Newcastle manager who was twice European football of the year and a stalwart member of Liverpool’s serial First Division and European champions in the 1970s, has died aged 75.

Keegan’s family revealed in January that he had cancer, and in June he revealed himself that it was stage four, the most advanced stage. “It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75,” read a family statement. “Kevin had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

“A double Ballon D’or winner, Kevin was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy.”

Keegan started his career at Scunthorpe before being signed for Liverpool by Bill Shankly for just £33,000 in 1971, “King Kevin” going on to win the First Division title three times as well as the FA Cup, the Uefa Cup twice and the 1977 European Cup. Keegan is the only British player to have won two Ballons d’Or.

The 5ft 8in combative “Mighty Mouse” was not, by his own admission, a natural talent but the son of a south Yorkshire miner trained hard, remained humble and never ducked a challenge, traits that endeared him to the Kop. “I learned so much from Shanks. He used to say: ‘If I was a road-sweeper, my street would be the cleanest in the borough.’ I took that to heart,’ he said.

Keegan was twice named European Footballer of the Year while at the German club Hamburg and returned to England to play for Southampton and Newcastle before retiring as a player in 1984. He won 63 England caps, scoring 21 goals, playing at the 1982 World Cup and was also captain at the 1980 Euros.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool’s Ian Callaghan, Kevin Keegan and Ray Clemence parade the winning trophy after the 1974 FA Cup final between Liverpool and Newcastle at Wembley. Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty Images

Keegan was never one to hold back, his fiery temperament rarely far from the surface. He was memorably sent off for scrapping with Leeds’s Billy Bremner in the 1974 Charity Shield after boiling over and his volatile temperament and pugnacious intolerance of football’s machinations, real or perceived. “I don’t like people to deceive me and tell me lies,” he told the Guardian in 2018.

View image in fullscreen Kevin Keegan in 2008. Photograph: Michael Mayhew/Sportsphoto

He wrote newspaper columns, was one of the English game’s first players to have their own branded football boots, had a hit record (Head Over Heels in Love), and became an enduring star of the BBC’s Superstars. He was the public face of 70s aftershave Brut 33 with Henry Cooper. He became close friends with another of the game’s renegades, George Best. “I wanted so much to have his ability. His skill was unbelievable. I played against Cruyff, Beckenbauer, Maradona. But I still say Besty was the best I played against,” he told Simon Hatterstone.

Keegan retired from playing aged 33 and moved to Spain, where his two daughters grew up unaware he had been a footballer. “It was the best decision I made in my life,” he told the Guardian in 2011. “I was at the highest level and the only way was down. I call it the glass mountain – you can’t climb a glass mountain.”

In 1992, Keegan made his first step into management at his former club Newcastle, guiding them into the Premier League and to within touching distance of the 1995-96 title only to miss out to Manchester United. His finger-jabbing “I will love it” rant when Alex Ferguson’s mind-games to get the better of him has become part of the English game’s lore.

After leaving St James’ Park in January 1997, a brief stint at Fulham followed before he became England manager in 1999, having initially taken on the job following Glenn Hoddle’s departure. Amid a disappointing Euro 2000 campaign, Keegan resigned on the back of defeat by Germany at Wembley Stadium, after just 20 months and 18 games, winning only seven of them – the worst win ratio of any England manager.

A spell at Manchester City followed, but Keegan left the club in March 2005, initially announcing his retirement from football, only to make an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008. That second spell lasted eight months following tensions with the board and owner Mike Ashley. In 2009 a tribunal awarded Keegan £2m damages for constructive dismissal.

View image in fullscreen Kevin Keegan loses his cool on Sky Sports in March 1996 reacting to ‘mind games’ by the Manchester United manager Alex Ferguson. Photograph: Sky Sports

He was made an OBE in 1982 for services to football, but Keegan’s unreconstructed opinions could offend. In 2023, his questioning the suitability of former England women’s internationals commenting on incidents in men’s international matches landed him in hot water. At a public event in Bristol, he told the audience: “I don’t like to listen to ladies talking about the England men’s team at the match because I don’t think it’s the same experience. I have a problem with that.”

This story will update

Sports.title: Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino booed before US president attempts to crash Spain celebrations
Sports.content:
Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino were booed as they took to the field for the presentation ceremony before the US president attempted to gatecrash Spain’s victory party.

Trump arrived at the stadium on Marine One, with the president’s helicopter first flying over the stadium about 45 minutes before kick-off. He sat in a glassed-in section of luxury seats for the match, along with Infantino. Other dignitaries and former players sat nearby, including Spain’s king, Felipe VI, Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, and Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum.

Trump was briefly shown on the video screens at the stadium after the US national anthem was played. There were scattered boos from some in the crowd but nothing like the hostile reception he has received at other sporting events during his presidency. However, when the US president and Infantino came on to the field for the presentation after Spain clinched victory, boos rang out around the stadium. The White House pool report said that ambient crowd noise, which had been sitting at approximately 78 decibels before their introduction, rose to 84 decibels when Trump entered the field.

Then, after Trump presented Spain with the World Cup trophy, he attempted to stand with the team at the side of the podium as they celebrated before Infantino quietly ushered him away.

It was a repeat of last summer’s Club World Cup at the same stadium after Trump presented the trophy to champions Chelsea and tried to crash the celebrations to the bemusement of the players.

Trump has made several appearances at sporting events since his re-election. Last year, he attended the Super Bowl, tennis’s US Open, the Daytona 500 and golf’s Ryder Cup. This year, he has attended several golf events, college football’s national championship game and Game 3 of the NBA finals, where he was met with boos from the New York Knicks home crowd.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi receives his runner-up medal from Donald Trump. Photograph: Alex Pantling/FIFA/Getty Images

Trump’s appearance was the first time he has attended a match at this summer’s World Cup, which the US have co-hosted along with Canada and Mexico.

At the 2022 World Cup final, the emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, joined Infantino to award the trophy to Lionel Messi and his Argentina teammates. Vladimir Putin awarded it to Kylian Mbappé and France after their win at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

View image in fullscreen Rodri lifts the World Cup Trophy alongside Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino. Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images

Trump is the first sitting US president to attend a World Cup final on home soil. When the US hosted the tournament in 1994, Trump’s predecessor Bill Clinton did not attend the game. The trophy was instead presented by Clinton’s vice-president, Al Gore.

Trump has a close relationship with Infantino, and called the Fifa president to lobby for a review of USA star Folarin Balogun’s controversial red-card suspension before their last-16 match. Fifa did reverse Balogun’s ban, but the political circus cast a pall over the US team, who exited a promising World Cup with defeat to Belgium.

Sports.title: Tuchel is clinging to an outdated English style – he must let players take risks | Jacob Steinberg
Sports.content:
Only England can claim the bronze medal at the World Cup by beating France in a 10-goal thriller and end up even more annoyed with the manager. Yet emotions are still running high after the collapse against Argentina last week and it is going to take more than winning a game low on jeopardy for the criticism of Thomas Tuchel to die down.

Hiring Tuchel was centred around the promise that he would make the difference in the big games. When that fell down, all that was left was anger. It exposed the core emptiness of the appointment, of a rich federation covering up the flaws in its coaching development by trying to game the system by throwing money at an expensive outsider.

What is the Football Association’s vision? The initial idea was Tuchel providing a short, sharp shock and his tactical acumen helping England to get over the line. Then came a change after a successful qualifying campaign against modest opposition. The FA moved the goalposts by handing Tuchel a contract extension, and suddenly winning the World Cup did not seem quite as pressing.

Yet the idea of Tuchel as a project builder seemed far-fetched during the bitter recriminations after the defeat by Argentina. Criticised for his negative substitutions when England led, the German talked dismissively of English DNA, lamenting the lack of care in possession. Fair enough, you thought, because this has long been a weakness – only, hadn’t Tuchel caused some of the damage by leaving out most of the ball players from his squad? Would it have been different if Adam Wharton, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer had been around in Atlanta? Maybe not, but a lot of money has been spent on developing a different type of English player in recent decades.

Perhaps Tuchel was thinking of an old English DNA. But maybe this is part of the issue with employing a foreign coach whose focus is on winning by any means possible. This is the third time England have been down this road. There is an idea of the manager from abroad as a sophisticate. But Sven-Göran Eriksson was not as tactically adroit as Glenn Hoddle. Eriksson played a traditional 4-4-2 whereas Hoddle was flexible with his formations.

Tuchel, too, has struggled to build an identity. He seems taken with an outdated English style. Tuchel wanted to play like a Premier League team, with pace and physicality, but that has rarely worked for England. They tend to be outpassed in big knockout games, which is why there has been such focus in youth football in developing players more at ease with the dominant Spanish passing style.

View image in fullscreen England players look dejected after the semi-final defeat by Argentina. Photograph: Paul Childs/Reuters

Spain have just won another World Cup, their method too much for Argentina in a dour final, and for those watching from afar a big takeaway will surely be that the last two teams standing were led by homegrown coaches.

Luis de la Fuente and Lionel Scaloni have risen through the ranks and are part of a system. They have a feeling for their countries, a sense of the identity. Tuchel has been inserted in the hope he can cover up the FA’s failure to produce its own coaches. No male team led by a foreign manager has secured the World Cup and it should worry the FA when bringing in an outsider with a win-now mentality ends with the senior side using a very different style of play to younger age groups.

There is a view within youth coaching circles that Tuchel has taken England backwards at this tournament. The under-21s have won the past two European Championships by being brave on the ball. They have beaten Spain in consecutive tournaments and the demand from Lee Carsley is that his players take risks in possession. Tuchel finished the semi-final by lobbing balls towards Dan Burn. He played a pragmatic style and his England ended up unable to throw caution to the wind. This World Cup underlines that turning to celebrated coaches from the club game is not a recipe for success.

Brazil appointed Carlo Ancelotti but went out in the last 16. Roberto Martínez failed with Portugal after sticking with Cristiano Ronaldo. Mauricio Pochettino oversaw the USA side being humiliated by Belgium.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Scaloni came through the national setup before winning the World Cup with Argentina in 2022. Similarly De la Fuente won the European Under-19 Championship with Spain in 2015 and the European Under-21 Championship in 2019. He has brought players through and, having earned a promotion, won the senior European title in 2024.

View image in fullscreen Luis de la Fuente was a successful age-group manager before taking over Spain’s senior side and leading them to glory. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

Spain show smooth progression. Players who beat Argentina in the final played youth football for De la Fuente. This is not to say that England’s next step should be to appoint Carsley, who did not seem as if he had the temperament for the senior job when he filled in as caretaker between Gareth Southgate’s departure and Tuchel’s arrival. Even so, Carsley is closer to the Spanish style and has shown it is possible for England teams to be risk-takers.

It is food for thought for the FA as it reviews England’s World Cup. As it stands, Tuchel will get another tournament. There are bridges to build but finishing third is not a sackable offence. In any case there is no other idea at the FA. Tuchel was not produced, he was bought. Hopefully he adapts during the Nations League. There should be a shift away from this physical style. But do not be surprised if the hired gun’s views on English DNA end up making him sound out of touch. It would not happen to Spain. De la Fuente knows their identity. He is part of it.

Sports.title: Hits, misses and Muppets: the star-studded World Cup half-time show nobody asked for
Sports.content:
Like hydration breaks and Donald Trump’s ability to get refereeing decisions overturned by simply phoning up the president of Fifa and complaining, the final half-time show is an innovation of the 2026 World Cup that comes with a degree of controversy attached. For one thing, its existence automatically means the World Cup final breaks the International Football Association’s 15-minute half-time mandate.

For another, its obvious antecedent lies in the NFL’s Super Bowl, where the half-time entertainment has mushroomed over the decades from a few marching bands to one of the big pop events of the year. To its detractors, it smacks of America not so much embracing the World Cup as imposing itself upon it.

View image in fullscreen Shakira performs during the World Cup final. Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images

But before you even got to the main event, there was more musical entertainment at the final to wade through, most notably the pre-match closing ceremony, a damp squib that neither the BBC nor ITV elected to broadcast live.

Anyone who hastened to iPlayer was rewarded not merely with Post Malone debuting what’s presumably the first single from his forthcoming album the Eternal Buzz, Chrome Heartbreaker (a pivot back to hip-hop-influenced pop after his recent diversion into country, should you be eagerly tracking the artistic vacillations of Post Malone’s career) and duetting with Swae Lee on their US chart-topper Sunflower, but also an online influencer-cum-professional wrestler called IShowSpeed performing Champions, a track that gained so much traction online that Fifa felt obliged to include it on the official Fifa World Cup album.

A frightful cocktail of thunderous drums and autotuned vocals, it featured lyrics that make your average football song sound as erudite and profound as the oeuvre of Leonard Cohen: “I take a breath and wait for the ref / This is the World Cup, put your hands in the air.” Alas, news of its social media virality clearly hadn’t reached the audience in the New York New Jersey Stadium. The deathly silence at its conclusion made you wonder if perhaps the TV broadcast couldn’t pick up the sound of the crowd, but no: some fireworks subsequently went off and they went audibly mental.

View image in fullscreen Three members of the Muppets’ house band the Electric Mayhem performed the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters

There was, it turned out, more to come. Jennifer Hudson sang the Star-Spangled Banner. Dutifully flogging a dead horse with all the professionalism he could muster, Robbie Williams performed the Fifa anthem, Desire, in the company of Laura Pausini and Nicole Scherzinger. The ballad debuted at the draw ceremony in December and – like all the musical entertainment at said event – it was overshadowed by the news that Fifa had apparently started making up awards in order to give them to Donald Trump. It vanished into obscurity thereafter, failing to chart anywhere in the world. Listening to it exhumed for another airing, you were forced to concede that the world had a point.

After all that, the actual half-time show felt like a comparative triumph. You could argue that the bar had been set pretty low without much dissent, but nonetheless, it zipped along, cramming a lot into its 11 minutes by the simple expedient of paring songs down to their bare essentials and swiftly cutting between artists. Madonna performed a version of her 2000 hit Music – reworked over a backing track immediately recognisable as derived from the Trammps’ Disco Inferno – on a vaguely Mad Max-ish vehicle piloted by Ronaldo and Ronaldinho.

Then the strains of the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army rang out, ostensibly performed by three members of the Muppets’ house band the Electric Mayhem. There was no sign of their leader, Dr Teeth, but perhaps he was indisposed, being treated backstage after being exposed to Champions by IShowSpeed. BTS rattled through Dynamite, Shakira and Burna Boy played a truncated version of Dai Dai – the solitary World Cup song in recent memory to actually impact on the British charts – and Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love accompanied by a children’s choir: the latter looks horrendous on paper, but was far less sugary in reality, undercut by the farty blast of a crowd of vuvuzela players.

View image in fullscreen Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love accompanied by a children’s choir that was far less sugary than it could have been. Photograph: Tullio Puglia/FIFA/Getty Images

The solitary misstep might have involved allowing Justin Bieber to perform a downcast acoustic ballad, Everything Hallelujah – viral hit following his performance at Coachella or not, this perhaps wasn’t the moment for introspection – but no matter: if the half-time show wasn’t sufficiently head-spinning to convince the viewer it should be a regular occurrence at every World Cup final, it worked well enough to justify its existence at least this time. Although clearly not everyone felt the same way: “I thought it was crap,” offered Wayne Rooney, when pressed for his opinions by BBC presenter Gabby Logan.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi’s World Cup fairytale ends with pitiful Argentina as final villains | Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Sports.content:
Playing on the grandest stage in sport for the last time, Lionel Messi seemed almost certain to provide one last memorable moment in this World Cup final.

Yet as the sun ducked behind the west stand of New York New Jersey Stadium on Sunday, it became clearer and clearer that Argentina had lost the magic they had carried through this tournament. And as Spain gradually wrested control, one was left to confront reality: Messi, and Argentina, had finally run out of time, having long since given in to their worst instincts in a 1-0 defeat.

This final presented a stark contrast to the Argentina – and Messi – we observed in every other match of the tournament. Almost without exception, La Albiceleste have been the tournament’s most entertaining team, not so much for how they’ve scored their goals but for when they’ve scored them, offering a masterclass in dramatic timing. Twice they were nearly eliminated by badly outmatched opponents, results that only galvanized them.

Finals are frequently forgettable matches that fail to entertain but even by that lowly standard the pacing of things felt dreadful. Spain were suffocating defensively and – after a forgettable first half – finally worked their way into things in the second 45, eventually breaking through in extra time, quite expectedly. Argentina? They became the first team in the near century-long history of the tournament to fail to record a shot in regular time of a World Cup final. Even when handed an additional half an hour, they never threatened.

And Messi? Until this final, he had presented observers with one of the rarest opportunities in professional sport: a chance to witness greatness free of stakes, entirely devoid of any real pressure to perform. At 39, Messi has done his time and nobody could criticize his collection of hardware – as an individual or as part of a club or country. This defeat does nothing to sully a spotless legacy; a win would have only strengthened his claim as the greatest player in the history of the sport. To some Argentinians, the victory against England in their semi-final likely carries nearly as much weight as a victory in the final would have.

Yet it has to be said: Messi was rarely involved in this match, a far cry from the player who has sometimes carried his team this summer. Much of this, of course, is down to a Spain masterclass in defending. That alone is not always enough to contain the diminutive Argentina captain. But give Spain their due: they badly outclassed Argentina in every way, neutralizing even Messi. By the end Argentina had become what so many observers pegged them to be in the first place, sometimes unfairly: underhanded, dirty and desperate.

Time has almost always been irrelevant to Messi on the field, because he so frequently bends it to his liking to elude those who defend him. The manner in which he performs at age 39 has a similar effect, tearing open a rift in time itself and transporting observers back to his glory days at Barcelona and elsewhere. Time itself has not passed him by as much as he’s marched alongside it, occasionally trailing behind a step or two but always eventually pulling even with it again.

View image in fullscreen Spain kept close tabs on Lionel Messi, who had little impact on the final. Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty Images

Yet now we are left to face the unmistakable reality that Messi is done, with the World Cup at least – this is, it’s worth noting, what was said after he led Argentina to their first World Cup in nearly four decades in 2022 and what was assumed in 2016, when Messi briefly retired from the national team after Argentina’s defeat in the Copa América final. Back then, the dialogue surrounding this player was that he would never play for Argentina the way he did for Barcelona, or even rumblings that Messi himself wasn’t sufficiently Argentinian, having spent so much of his life in Spain. Both arguments feel laughable 10 years later.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It remains to be seen how Argentina’s performance will be perceived back home, where expectations were understandably high. The head coach, Lionel Scaloni, and even Messi had spoken at length before the final about how much they had already achieved. This final result, they implied, would do little to sully that sense of accomplishment.

This was, of course, before they took the field and more or less destroyed the game. Scaloni’s legacy, like Messi’s, was secure before this final, the coach having brought Argentina a third World Cup and a pair of Copa América titles, but this was a lost opportunity to solidify it. Two things can coexist: Scaloni is almost without question Argentina’s greatest coach, and this was one of his worst results and performances.

What feels much more real, though, is a sense of loss and disappointment after this pitiful final performance, which provided Argentina – and Messi – with a perfect opportunity to put the finishing touches on their fairytale. Instead, they turned from hero to villain – and needlessly so.

Sports.title: Melvine Malard hungry for trophies after joining Chelsea from Manchester United
Sports.content:
Chelsea have announced the signing of the France forward Melvine Malard from Manchester United on a four-year contract. The Guardian revealed last week that a deal was close for the 26-year-old, who has left United after three seasons for about £850,000.

Malard had one year on her contract and United were keen to keep the forward. However, once it became clear Malard wanted a move United decided to sell rather than lose a high-value player on a free next summer.

It is believed United will reinvest the fee, which is a record sale for the club, into the squad, with the transfer window open until 3 September.

United have made one summer signing, the full-back Andrea Medina from Atlético Madrid, but more incomings are expected after the departures of Leah Galton, Hannah Blundell, Sienna Wareing, Millie Turner, Lisa Naalsund and Malard.

“I’m so happy because I have a plan for my life and my career, and Chelsea were a part of that plan,” Malard said. ”My objective is to become better every single day and to win trophies. I know Chelsea always have that as an objective.”

The France international played under Chelsea’s head coach, Sonia Bompastor, at Lyonnes (formerly Lyon) and was recruited to their academy by Bompastor. “I have known Sonia since I was 14 years old, so it is great to work with her again,” Malard said.

It is understood Chelsea have been tracking Malard for some time. They have lost a number of players across the forward line, with the club record-goalscorer Sam Kerr and Guro Reiten departing for Gotham FC, Catarina Macario joining San Diego Wave and Johanna Rytting Kaneryd signing for Lyonnes.

Malard is Chelsea’s third signing of the summer, after the former Arsenal full-back Katie McCabe and the forward Manaka Matsukubo, who was with North Carolina Courage.

Malard spent seven seasons at Lyonnes, winning four Champions Leagues, three league titles and two Coupes de France. Her first season with United was on loan.

Last season she scored four goals in United’s run to a first Champions League quarter-final and six times in 18 Women’s Super League games.

Liverpool have signed the Japanese attacking midfielder Mao Itamura from Feyenoord. The 19-year-old, who won the Under-20 Women’s Asian Cup in April, was the Eredivisie player of the year last season in the Netherlands. She scored eight times and provided six assists as Feyenoord qualified for European competition for the first time, their third-place finish earning a place in the Europa Cup.

Itamura is Liverpool’s fifth summer signing, after Vivien Endemann, Sara Agrez, Mari Ward and Khiara Keating.

Sports.title: Rodri’s redemption story leaves stars in the shadow of Spain’s great controller | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
You don’t need to be long in the US before somebody, finding you’re here to cover “the Fifa” as so many Americans so demoralisingly call it, will tell you that the USA would obviously win it all the time if only their best athletes weren’t distracted by more local pursuits: American football, basketball, eating enormous sandwiches and the like. If you’re really lucky they’ll start shouting names at you with a detailed rundown of height, weight, sprint speed, what they can bench and other fascinating statistics.

At which you wonder whether the 5ft 7in Lionel Messi has ever done a bench press. Rodri probably has, but he’s still nobody’s idea of a great athlete. He’s tall without being physically imposing. He’s not quick. He ambles about games being in the right place. Occasionally he leans into people or passes the ball 10 yards. It would be difficult to put together a highlights reel of his performance in the World Cup final that would convince a neophyte that he was the defining player – but he was, and was rightly named player of the tournament as well.

This has been a World Cup in which individual stars shone. Kylian Mbappé topped the goalscoring charts, followed by Messi, Jude Bellingham, Erling Haaland, Harry Kane and Ousmane Dembélé. In the most heavily marketed World Cup ever, there were plenty of faces to market: “Look at this celebrity, scoring a goal!” But in the end the parade of goalscorers ended up marching in the shadow of the great controller.

Mauricio Pochettino made the point last year that there were two problems with a US system that in effect forces a parent who wants their child to play soccer to pay thousands of dollars a year to belong to a club. The first is that it means huge swathes of the population are excluded for basic financial reasons. The second is less obvious but perhaps almost as insidious: parents at the end of the year will demand to see progress, to know what they’ve got for their money.

The two most important attributes for an elite footballer – technical ability and tactical awareness – are extremely difficult to measure. And so coaches tend to tell parent that their charge has knocked a fraction off their sprint time, or is lifting 20 pounds more. That’s measurable; it satisfies the need to see a return on investment. The result is a focus on physicality rather than the nebulous but vital skills that define the best players, something reflected in how the US play. Carli Lloyd made a similar point, and a series of youth coaches I’ve spoken to over the past month have agreed.

View image in fullscreen Rori directs traffic in the Spain midfield during Sunday’s World Cup final. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters

There is no American Rodri, and perhaps in the present system there cannot be one. But then there is no English Rodri, or French Rodri, or Argentinian Rodri, or German Rodri. Rodri is a very Spanish type. He comes from the line of Sergio Busquets, and the closest player to him in the modern game is Martín Zubimendi. In an environment in which football is becoming increasing physical, they have found a role for the cerebral.

Much of what Rodri does is indefinable. He didn’t score a goal or register an assist at this World Cup. A pass completion rate of 93.2% is obviously very good, but it was only the 44th best in the tournament. Even if you filter out centre-backs, who play a lot of short simple, unpressured passes, Rodri is 18th. He ranked 22nd for tackles per game and 450th for interceptions. Even at fouling, at which, following in the proud Manchester City lineage of Fernandinho, Rodri is a master, has was only 97th. Although he completed a record 756 passes at this tournament, his great skill is simply being. By existing in the right spaces, Rodri lubricates and distributes and, by somehow combining that with a capacity to draw matter towards him, he discourages opponents from passing in his zone. He, as much as anyone, was the reason Lionel Messi was so little involved in the final.

Yet as recently as the end of the domestic season – which admittedly doesn’t feel that recent after 104 World Cup games, but was only two months ago – there were doubts about whether Rodri would ever be quite the same again. It was only 10 weeks after being named player of the tournament at Euro 2024 that Rodri sustained the anterior crucial ligament injury that kept him out for the 2024-25 season. City’s decline in his absence told its own story.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

His return was not straightforward. He struggled during the Club World Cup, forced off during the defeat by Al-Hilal. He started only 17 league games last season. Pep Guardiola suggested that the best of Rodri wouldn’t be seen until the World Cup. That’s been a recurring theme; most of the best players at this tournament were those who had not slogged through 50+ high-intensity games last season.

In that sense, Rodri’s is a great redemption story, a player returning after two very difficult seasons to add World Cup honours to his European award. But there’s also an undeniable irony that in a country that celebrates the individual like no other, in a World Cup that has relentlessly promoted celebrities, the defining player ends up being the most unflashy team-oriented candidate imaginable, the first non-creator to win the Golden Ball in 24 years.

Sports.title: Farewell to 'Mighty Mouse' Kevin Keegan - the diminutive pioneer who let his emotions run wild and was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan, a kid from mining stock in South Yorkshire, a kid who started out at Scunthorpe United and went on to conquer Europe, was one of the greatest players English football has ever produced but it was the unquenchable passion that burned within him that won him such a prominent place in the hearts of the public.

Mighty Mouse, he was called as a player and it suited him. He was the little man who would never give up. He was the small guy who punched way above his weight. He was the lad who never bowed to anyone. He may have been slight of stature but he had the biggest heart that ever beat in the chest of an English footballer.

Sometimes, it feels as if time has dimmed the memory of quite what an outstanding footballer Keegan was and how he became a pioneer and a pathfinder, the first Englishman to play in a European Cup final with both English and foreign clubs, in his case Liverpool and Hamburger SV.

Sometimes it feels as if England’s mediocrity when he was at the peak of his playing career and the fame and affection he garnered in his managerial career, particularly at Newcastle United, have obscured the fact that he remains the only Englishman to have won the Ballon d’Or, the prize bestowed on the greatest player in the world each year, more than once.

Keegan won it in successive years during his time in Germany, in 1978 and 1979. For context, that puts him level with Franz Beckenbauer, Alfredo Di Stefano, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge and the Brazilian Ronaldo in the pantheon of the greats of the game. ‘I’m probably the most ordinary player to have won it twice,’ Keegan said in a recent interview.

But there was nothing ordinary about Kevin Keegan. Anybody who ever met him or ever watched him play or ever heard him giving a manager’s post-match press conference or ever saw him spending hours with fans desperate for a word or an autograph, knew that.

Kevin Keegan has tragically passed away at the age of 75 after a short battle with illness

Keegan (pictured in 1977 after winning the European Cup with Liverpool ) is one of the greatest players English football has ever produced

Once, after his playing career was over, I sat opposite him on a stage at Westminster Central Hall, asking him questions in an interview organised by the newspaper I worked for then. I don’t remember the questions I asked, or the answers he gave.

What I do remember is how Keegan held the audience in the palm of his hand. They were rapt. After it was over, Keegan stayed until he had fulfilled every autograph request and spoken to every man and woman who wanted a word, who wanted to say that they had talked to one of the legends of the English game.

Keegan was an extraordinary man. He was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world. In a sport where players are told to keep their mouths shut and their emotions in check, he let his emotions run wild and people loved him for it.

His public profile rose even more when he competed in the BBC programme Superstars, which aired in the 1970s and 80s, and featured sportsmen battling it out against each other in series of different disciplines.

‘Superstar’ has become an overused term now but if ever a man fitted that description, it was Keegan. He was box office, from head to toe. The combination of the reach of television and the dynamism of his personality made him one of football’s first new age icons.

Even in the midst of everything he achieved on the pitch, what endeared him to people, and a huge part of the gift he leaves behind for us, was his heart and soul. His passion lit up his life. He could not contain it and we loved him for it.

His passion gave us some of the landmarks we remember him for. The fight with Leeds United captain Billy Bremner at the 1974 Charity Shield that got both men sent off and saw Keegan ripping off his shirt as he left the pitch.

What a different world it was then. ‘That looked very much like a right hook by Johnny Giles,’ commentator Barry Davies said when Keegan was flattened by a sweet right hand. Keegan pleaded for leniency for Giles. A few moments later, he was trading punches with Bremner. ‘This is a side of English football we do not want to see,’ Davies opined.

Keegan, who was born in Doncaster, had begun his career with Scunthorpe United before he was spotted and scouted by Liverpool manager Bill Shankly and established himself as the star player of the team that went on to win the European Cup, under Bob Paisley, in 1977.

That team was one of the great sides in the history of the English game. Let the names roll off your tongue: Ray Clemence, Phil Neal, Joey Jones, Tommy Smith, Ray Kennedy, Emlyn Hughes, Kevin Keegan, Jimmy Case, Steve Heighway, Ian Callaghan, Terry McDermott.

Keegan tormented the Borussia Monchengladbach captain Berti Vogts in that final in Rome and won the penalty in the 83rd minute that sealed a 3-1 victory for Liverpool and was the start of the club’s rise to being the most successful club in European competition in this country.

When Keegan moved to Hamburger SV that summer, many thought it would mark the end of Liverpool’s hegemony but they signed a player called Kenny Dalglish, who went on to emulate Keegan’s successes and more.

Then there was his bike crash in Superstars when he peddled furiously down the main straight of an athletics track at the start of a race against Belgian footballer, Gilbert Van Binst, wobbling from side to side as he desperately tried to keep up, before crashing to the tarmac on the first bend.

It was a nasty accident. Keegan, who was close to the height of his powers as a footballer at that point, sustained cuts and grazes but he still refused to give up. The race was re-started and Keegan won. It was the show’s greatest moment.

Keegan was an extraordinary man. He was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world

Keegan became a hugely successful manager and is particularly adored by Newcastle fans

Keegan pictured in 1995 with famous entertainers Ant McPartlin (L) and Declan Donnelly (R)

Then there was the most famous diatribe in English football history when, feeling the hot despair of Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United closing in on the league title after they had overhauled his wonderful Newcastle United team, he snapped as he spoke to Sky Sports after an away win over Leeds United at Elland Road at the end of April 1996.

‘We’re still fighting for this title,’ Keegan almost shouted into the camera, his voice shaking with anger and his finger pointing and jabbing, ‘and he (Sir Alex Ferguson) has got to go to Middlesbrough and get something and I’ll tell you honestly, I will love it if we beat them. Love it.’

David Beckham has said since that when the United players watched Keegan’s rant, they knew they had won the league. They knew that Ferguson’s mind games had exploded in Keegan’s head and that the title was theirs.

But that only added to Keegan’s legend. There was something magnificently untameable about him, something beautifully unpredictable, something free and untrammelled. He was still Mighty Mouse.

And he is still adored in Newcastle. It may be, in fact, that he is adored there more than anywhere else. He is adored for the pride he brought to the city and the way he resurrected the club and for the thrill of the beautiful football the Geordies played under his management.

That team was made in his image and so it was brilliant and it was entertaining and it was breathtaking but it was also fragile. And it could not quite cope with the relentlessness of Manchester United. But every neutral was desperate for Newcastle to win the title that season. And that was mostly down to Keegan.

There was no artifice about Keegan. He did not bother to try to hide what he was feeling. Or what he was. It was all out there, everything worn on his sleeve. He would have been the world’s worst poker player. He was not a man for keeping his counsel. Or for keeping his cool. Again, we loved him all the more for that.

Keegan always burned hot. At his unveiling as England manager in 1999, Daily Mirror journalist Nigel Clarke, who was sitting on the front row of the press conference, coughed while Keegan was speaking. Keegan became convinced that Clarke was mocking him and demanded to know why he was coughing. A long stand-off ensued.

Before a game against Sweden the same year, Keegan told Paul Scholes to ‘go out there and drop a few hand grenades’. Scholes promptly became the first England player to be sent off at Wembley after two horrendous challenges on opponents.

At the end of his short reign as England boss, Keegan was preparing his team for the final game at the old Wembley on October 7, 2000, a World Cup qualifier against Germany, and he decided he was going to play Gareth Southgate, a central defender in midfield.

On the Friday night before the game on the Saturday, the news began to leak out. I was on a Sky programme called Hold the Back Page, hosted by Brian Woolnough and Jimmy Hill, and we began the show by discussing the Southgate plan with varying degrees of scepticism.

Keegan was incandescent. He asked the FA to phone Sky to demand that the programme be taken off the air. Sky, obviously, could not accede to that request and the show continued as normal. To no one’s great surprise, the Southgate experiment did not go well.

Keegan managed England from February 1999 to October 2000 but resigned from his post

Keegan won the Ballon d'Or in successive years during his time playing for Hamburger SV

England lost the game 1-0 and Keegan was booed by a section of England fans as he walked off the pitch. He stopped to remonstrate with some of them at the entrance to the tunnel. When he reached the dressing rooms, he summoned FA officials, retreated to the quiet of the toilets, and promptly resigned. The FA tried to talk him out of it but he would not reconsider.

Keegan had been a sublime player at Liverpool and Hamburger SV and then, in the late summer of his career with Southampton and Newcastle. I say late summer deliberately. There was never anything autumn about Keegan. His football did not yellow and fade. After his last game for Newcastle, a testimonial against Liverpool, he was lifted from the St James’s Park pitch in a helicopter.

‘Auf Wiedersehen, Kev,’ a message on the scoreboard at the Gallowgate End read that day in May 1984. And now, it is time to bid him farewell once more. Auf Wiedersehen, Kev, and thank you.

Sports.title: Football world mourns Kevin Keegan: Heartbroken Alan Shearer pays tribute to his 'hero' while Jamie Carragher hails 'one of the greatest players this country has ever produced'
Sports.content:
Football world mourns Kevin Keegan: Heartbroken Alan Shearer pays tribute to his 'hero' while Jamie Carragher hails 'one of the greatest players this country has ever produced'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Alan Shearer has led the tributes to football legend Kevin Keegan after he passed away at the age of 75 following a short battle with illness.

Keegan was diagnosed with stage four stomach cancer in January, having been admitted to hospital with abdominal problems.

In a statement, his family said: 'It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75. The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

'Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy.'

And following the tragic news, figures from across the footballing world were quick to pay their respects to Keegan, who represented Scunthorpe, Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle and later managed the Magpies (twice), Fulham, England and Manchester City.

Newcastle legend Shearer said: 'My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss.'

Jamie Carragher has led the tributes to football legend Kevin Keegan (pictured after winning the European Cup with Liverpool in 1977) after he passed away

Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher added: 'RIP Kevin Keegan. One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies & goals galore, double Ballon d'Or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game.

'One of the most important men in making @LFC what it is today.'

Several of Keegan's former clubs also shared their own tribute, including Newcastle.

Posting on social media, they said: 'We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club’s history.

'Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.'

Liverpool shared their own heartfelt post which read: 'We are deeply saddened by the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan and mourn his loss.

'His indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on. Rest in peace, Kevin. 1951-2026.'

Keegan, a forward in his playing days, also won 63 caps for England before he later managed the Three Lions.

And they also posted a tribute which said: 'We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away.

'Kevin earned 63 international caps and scored 21 goals between 1972 and 1982, before managing the #ThreeLions from 1999 to 2000.

'Our thoughts and condolences are with Kevin's family, friends and former clubs.'

Former Newcastle owner Mehrdad Ghodoussi added: 'Devastated to hear about Kevin Keegan. Growing up watching football, he was one of the names that defined an era, a double Ballon d’Or winner, European Cup champion, England captain, and one of the most exciting players the game has seen.

'But what he did at Newcastle was different. He turned belief into something you could feel in the stadium.

'King Kev wasn’t just admired, he was loved, because everything he did came from the heart. Rest in peace, Kevin. Thank you for everything you gave the game.'

During his managerial career, Keegan also took Fulham from the Second Division (now League One) to the First Division (now Championship).

And the Cottagers also shared some words for the footballing legend as they said: 'We're incredibly sad to hear the news that our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away.

'A legend of the game, Keegan led Fulham to the Football League Second Division title in 1999. He left Craven Cottage at the end of that season to focus on his duties as England manager.

'Our thoughts are with his friends and family at this difficult time.'

MORE TO FOLLOW

Sports.title: Argentina and Tottenham defender Cristian Romero SNUBS Donald Trump after collecting World Cup runners-up medal
Sports.content:
Argentina and Tottenham defender Cristian Romero completely ignored US President Donald Trump after collecting his World Cup runners-up medal.

Trump joined FIFA chief Gianni Infantino to present various awards to players and match officials on stage following Spain's 1-0 World Cup final win over Argentina in extra time.

Before presenting the World Cup trophy to Spain captain Rodri, the pair handed out silver medals to runners-up Argentina.

After receiving his medal around his neck from Infantino, Romero snubbed Trump by not shaking his hand, instead he walked straight past him to join his team-mates.

The cold shoulder was spotted by fans with footage circulating on social media.

Argentina defender Cristian Romero snubbed President Donald Trump after collecting medal

Cristian Romero airing Trump.



Fair play.



pic.twitter.com/hn1jok7jUR — Out of Context Football Manager (@nocontextfm1) July 19, 2026

Trump then went on to ignore a call by Infantino to leave the stage at MetLife Stadium as Spain lifted the World Cup trophy.

The US President presented the prestigious title to Spain captain Rodri, who took great pleasure in raising it aloft in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Much like when he presented the Club World Cup title last summer, Trump stood awkwardly alongside the Spain squad as they lifted the trophy and celebrated wildly.

It seemed as though, when Spain were about to perform the trophy lift, Infantino had attempted to usher Trump away from the players - though the President remained.

He stood to the side of the squad as the confetti cannons went off at MetLife Stadium, clapping and grinning while Infantino laughed off Trump's awkward cameo.

There were an estimated 1.5-1.8 billion viewers tuning in to watch the summer tournament's showpiece finale, where Trump and Infantino took center stage once again.

Loud boos had come from the stands when Infantino and Trump made their way onto the pitch, as fans made their feelings on the duo undoubtedly clear.

The presentation came after Ferran Torres struck in the 106th minute with the decisive goal.

It was Spain who dominated the final and looked the most likely winners as disruptors Argentina committed 24 fouls and saw Enzo Fernandez sent off at the end of normal time.

Trump took center stage as Spain lifted the World Cup trophy on Sunday

It appeared as though FIFA chief Gianni Infantino attempted to usher Trump away - but the President remained

Join the discussion Should athletes use the world stage to make statements by snubbing political figures at major events?

But the European champions could not make the breakthrough until the second half of extra time when Torres smashed home from close range.

It was enough to seal the ultimate prize in football but when the final whistle blew the game descended into ugly scenes.

Some of Argentina's players lost their heads as Spain's substitutes and staff ran on to the pitch to celebrate their 1-0 win against the South Americans.

Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes was sent off for punching Eric Garcia and pushing Gavi to the ground.

Argentina's Nahuel Molina also punched Rodri in the torso as he was running by, while Thiago Almada was involved, too.

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan dead at 75: Football legend passes away following battle with cancer as devastated family pay heartbreaking tribute to England icon
Sports.content:
Newcastle and England legend Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75 after a short battle with illness.

Keegan was diagnosed with stage four stomach cancer in January, having been admitted to hospital with abdominal problems.

In a statement, his family said: 'It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

'The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

'Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support.

'This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy.'

Keegan leaves behind his wife, Jean, and their two daughters. Keegan met Jean on the Waltzers at Doncaster fair in 1970. They married four years later and had two daughters.

Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75 after a short battle with illness

Former England manager Keegan was diagnosed with stomach cancer in January this year

Keegan was a formidable footballer and twice won the Ballon d'Or - football's most prestigious individual prize - during his career

He won 63 caps for England and scored 21 goals across his 10-year international career

As a Liverpool player, Keegan delivered European glory for the Anfield club in 1977

Keegan posing during a photoshoot while at the peak of his footballing powers. He was renowned for his 'poodle perm' hair in the 1970s

Keegan pictured with his wife Jean, who was by his side when he died on Monday

Keegan at Buckingham Palace with his wife Jean and daughter Laura after being awarded an OBE in 1982

Keegan was admitted to hospital due to 'ongoing abdominal symptoms', a statement from his family said in January.

'These investigations have revealed a diagnosis of cancer, for which Kevin will undergo treatment,' it added.

However, he looked sprightly when he returned to public life in May. Keegan told an audience in Newcastle that he was responding well to treatment after being assured 'we have a top doctor with this new way of fighting what you have got'.

'He [the doctor] was a Liverpool supporter, so I went to meet him. I knew I wouldn't be walking alone, if you know what I mean.'

Keegan began his playing career at Scunthorpe in 1968, before moving to Liverpool to play for Bill Shankly three years later.

Keegan negotiated a contract worth £50 a week - Shankly had originally offered him £45.

It marked the beginning of a glorious playing career where he won 63 caps for England - captaining the Three Lions on 31 occasions.

The attacker won the First Division three times, the European Cup once and the UEFA Cup twice during a six-year stint at Liverpool.

🗣️ "I WILL LOVE IT IF WE BEAT THEM, LOVE IT!"



We have lost an English football legend today 😢💔 pic.twitter.com/YWo87RCnUV — The 44 ⚽️ (@The_Forty_Four) July 20, 2026

After retiring from football in 1985, Keegan turned to management and was at the helm of his beloved Newcastle United for five years (pictured with Ant and Dec in 1995)

His 'I would love it' meltdown saw Newcastle's Premier League title charge fall aprt

Keegan also managed England but handed in his resignation in the Wembley tunnel

He then moved to Germany to play for Hamburg and was named European Footballer of the Year in both 1978 and 1979. He added to the trophy cabinet in Germany, too, winning the Bundesliga and reaching the 1980 European Cup final.

Doncaster-born Keegan returned home after three years in Germany and spent time at Southampton and Newcastle - who he would later go on to manage. He rounded off his playing days with two appearances for Australian semi-professional side Blacktown City.

Keegan scored 204 goals in 592 career appearances across six clubs in a stellar career.

Alongside being iconic on the pitch, he produced his fair share of legendary moments off it too.

While Newcastle boss in 1996, Keegan launched a tirade on Manchester United during the heat of the Premier League title race.

Newcastle had let a 12-point lead slip at the top of the table with United moving six points clear after beating 10-man Leeds United 1-0 in April 1996.

Leeds played the majority of the game with defender Lucas Radebe in goal, which prompted Sir Alex Ferguson to question the Yorkshire side's integrity and whether they would show the same grit against Keegan’s Newcastle.

Newcastle responded by beating Leeds 1-0 to move three points behind Man Utd with a match in hand, and only two left to play.

But Keegan let the pressure of the title race get to him in his post-match interview, accusing United of being ‘slanderous’ and screaming ‘I will love it if we beat them, love it’.

In 1999 Keegan succeeded Glenn Hoddle as England boss but resigned in 2000 following a disappointing European Championship and a loss to Germany in the final match at the old Wembley.

His managerial career produced its fair share of bizarre moments. After a year and eight months as England manager, Keegan famously resigned in the tunnel at the old Wembley after a drab 1-0 defeat to Germany in October 2000.

Following a brutal reception from the England fans, he told his players in the dressing room that he was stepping down before confirming his resignation to FA director David Davies in a nearby stadium toilet cubicle.

He guided Newcastle to the Football League First Division title during the first of two stints at St James' Park and came close to lifting the Premier League, only to be pipped by Manchester United.

He would go on to oversee promotions to the top flight for both Fulham and City.

Sports.title: I was at Kevin Keegan's last public appearance in Newcastle in May with hundreds of adoring fans. Although ill, he still had that electric smile and was cheeky, inspirational and funny. A people person in full flow who will be desperately missed
Sports.content:
Simon Bird saw Kevin Keegan entertain fans in Newcastle on May 31 of this year. This is the piece Daily Mail Sport published at the time. The doctor told Kevin Keegan that he had a tremendous strike-rate at tackling the cancer that, last Christmas, left the former England manager floored, confined to bed and his family tearful. Here is Keegan, 75, entertaining on stage in Newcastle – more a congregation than an audience – speaking publicly for the first time about his diagnosis. He softens his concerning news with humour and the lexicon of his goal-scoring trade. 'I said: "Fantastic! What is your strike rate?" He said: "33 per cent". Oh. I thought he might say 80, maybe 90! Anyway, I am still here at the moment…' Keegan, remarkably, is delivering a romp through his career with the aplomb of a stand-up comic. Jokes, old stories, that bike crash on Superstars, the Brut advert with Henry Cooper, the perms, road safety adverts, and sending himself up about the number of companies who sponsored him and then went bust. Peter Beardsley arrives to surprise his old strike partner and manager. Even Sir Ian Botham, who also played for Scunthorpe United, is in the audience. Keegan is in such lively form it is hard to believe it is only five months since he began treatment for stomach cancer, discovered 'luckily' after a car accident after which he needed a body scan. There is something special about the presence of Keegan in a room in Newcastle. It’s almost religious. Messianic. A football leadership version of Tony Blair selling a vision. There is something special about the presence of Kevin Keegan. It’s almost religious. Messianic Remember his head tennis duet with Tony Blair in 1995? 'We got to 22, turns out he was really good at it,' Keegan told the audience Keegan, remarkably, is delivering a romp through his career with the aplomb of a stand-up comic Remember their head tennis duet in 1995? 'We got to 22, turns out he was really good at it,' Keegan told the audience. He’s still inspirational, giving hope with his positivity. To Newcastle fans, especially, he’s the living embodiment of rebirth and reinvention of their club. Not once, but twice. As a player, and manager. Saved the club from relegation to the third tier, promotions, Premier League runners up. Some 6,000 fans watched training every day because there was a public footpath through the pitches: 'No need for Spygate in those days,' he laughed. 'Sir John Hall, the chairman, made the most of it and put in some burger vans!' If he could change anything, he says, it would be not getting wound up by Sir Alex Ferguson. Love it. Cancer? Facing mortality? Not Keegan, surely. But here he is explaining his own, traumatic few months. People sometimes say to him: 'Did you use to be Kevin Keegan?' Study the grey-haired man on the stage being serenaded, and it’s still the Kevin Keegan. Darting, diminutive striker rejected for being too small as a kid. The electric smile, cheeky, funny and human. A people person. The words flowing so naturally, spreading warmth. But there are words coming no one wants to hear: 'They said we have a top doctor with this new way of fighting what you have got. Which is stage-four cancer. He was a Liverpool supporter so I went to meet him. I knew I wouldn’t be walking alone, if you know what I mean.' Keegan revealed in January that he was ill. In April, after a 'really tough time' he was feeling well enough to commit to this appearance at the Tyne Theatre, near the Gallowgate End that he used to salute. This is a man who has achieved almost everything possible in football. England striker with 63 caps, 31 as skipper, scoring 21 goals and playing at the 1982 World Cup. A Liverpool legend with three league titles, an FA Cup win, a European Cup and two UEFA Cups. He won the Bundesliga with Hamburg, and the Ballon d’Or, one of only four Englishmen to do so. This is a man who has achieved almost everything possible in football. A Liverpool legend with three league titles, an FA Cup win, a European Cup and two UEFA Cups Keegan with the 1977 European Cup and a black eye after beating Borussia Monchengladbach in the final in Rome. It was Liverpool's first of six times winning the competition He won the Bundesliga with Hamburg, and the Ballon d’Or, one of only four Englishmen to do so As a manager, there was the Newcastle revival and the Great Entertainers, just in time to be part of the Premier League’s burgeoning riches. He turned Manchester City’s fortunes managing 176 games, and his 18 months with England ended after defeat by Germany in the final game at Wembley in 2000. Flawed at times? Yes, by his own admission. Too emotional when the chips were down? Maybe, but what fan would criticise a heart being worn on a sleeve? His was a career rich in medals and played out at the top. Financial riches, yes, but nothing like the fortune that a middle of the road Premier League star would command these days. As the Harry Kane of his day, Keegan could have expected to retreat into his world of loyal family, wife Jean and two daughters. But always an entrepreneur he finds the zest for life to entertain a few hundred die-hards a Sunday night in May. He’s not done yet. Perhaps the wider footballing public outside of Newcastle and Liverpool, and new generations of fans, can appreciate his mercurial, historically significant career, the trophies, near misses and fragile moments. Sir Kevin? Reminiscing, he is asked to wonder how a striker force of Keegan, Beardsley and Chris Waddle would fare these days? A quip, again: 'I’m not sure… probably struggle a bit. I’m not very fit at the moment.' He doesn’t want a statue at St James’ Park, alongside Sir Bobby Robson’s and Alan Shearer’s. 'You will have to wait until I die,' he says. 'My statue is the way people receive me.' He doesn’t want a statue at St James’s Park, alongside Sir Bobby Robson’s and Alan Shearer’s He will return to St James’ Park for the first time since an ill-fated spell as boss in 2008, next season, to wave to the crowd before kick off As Keegan continues his treatment, there could not have been any better therapy than a room full of mutual love and adulation
