World.title: Andy Burnham becomes U.K. prime minister
World.content:
Andy Burnham becomes U.K. prime minister

toggle caption Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP

LONDON — Keir Starmer is out. Andy Burnham is in.

On Monday, outgoing Prime Minister Starmer traveled to Buckingham Palace to tender his resignation to King Charles III. Shortly afterward, his successor, Andy Burnham, made the same journey and was invited by the king to form a new government.

Burnham then returned to Downing Street, where he delivered his first remarks as prime minister. He said, "It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game." He said politicians are "acknowledging that many voters have grown frustrated with politics."

"I want to be honest with you: We have not been good enough, and we need to be better. We will be," Burnham said.

Burnham becomes the U.K.'s seventh prime minister in a decade, since Britons voted in June 2016 to leave the European Union. That decision ultimately shrank the British economy, triggered anger at the governing class and contributed to a revolving door of prime ministers.

Sponsor Message

Starmer exits after two years

Starmer delivered his final speech outside No. 10 Downing St. earlier on Monday before heading to Buckingham Palace to formally resign as prime minister, declaring: "My work is done."

"In 6 1/2 years, I took our party from a historic defeat in 2019, changed it so it was fit to face the country, and won a landslide general election victory in 2024," Starmer said. He described serving as prime minister as "the privilege of my life" and said he was leaving office confident Britain was "stronger and fairer" than it was two years ago.

toggle caption Aaron Chown/Pool Photo via AP

Closing his final address outside Downing Street, Starmer said, "I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything we have achieved."

Starmer led the U.K.'s center-left Labour Party to a landslide victory two years ago. But his personal approval ratings sank. Polls show voters believe he failed to deliver palpable change. He was also criticized for appointing Peter Mandelson, a close friend of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, as British ambassador to Washington. Starmer later fired Mandelson.

After Labour lost seats to a populist anti-immigration party in May's local elections, more of Starmer's own lawmakers joined calls for his removal.

Sponsor Message

Starmer resigned as Labour leader on June 22, and Burnham assumed that role on Friday. Under Britain's parliamentary system, the ruling party can replace its leader — and therefore the prime minister — without a general election. The next election is not expected for another three years.

Burnham's first remarks as prime minister

Burnham previously served as a member of Parliament for 16 years, holding several Cabinet roles in the Labour governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown. He ran twice for the Labour leadership, receiving a nomination from Starmer during the 2015 contest, before leaving Parliament to become mayor of Greater Manchester.

As mayor, Burnham championed investment and devolution in the post-industrial region and has pledged to bring a similar approach to the U.K. nationally. He returned to Parliament in a special election last month.

Standing outside Downing Street, Burnham said he will announce measures to help with the cost of living on Tuesday, promising immediate support for households while setting out plans for longer-term change.

The new prime minister said his government would be "a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years."

"I can do something to give people some breathing space now, some help with the cost of living," Burnham said.

He added, "I will soon go through that door behind me and issue my first instruction: to end rough sleeping in our country." Burnham also said he would unveil a 10-year plan for Britain later this year.

A new prime minister, familiar challenges

Born and raised in the grittier north of England, Burnham has cultivated a working-class hero vibe, often wearing T-shirts rather than suits and advocating for blue-collar workers. He moonlights as a DJ on Manchester's indie music scene. His social media videos have been compared to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's.

Polls show he's one of the most popular U.K. politicians.

Sponsor Message

In terms of policy, Burnham has said he'll scrap plans for digital ID cards, reverse the privatization of public transit and utilities, and devolve power away from the capital, London, toward municipal and regional authorities.

In recent days, there have been reports that Burnham might ease a ban on new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea — which won him immediate praise from President Trump on social media on Sunday. Trump wrote that with North Sea drilling, Burnham would transform the U.K. from "a Poverty Stricken Disaster, to one of the Richest Countries anywhere in the World!"

European leaders have begun congratulating Andy Burnham on becoming the U.K.'s new prime minister, with an invitation for his first foreign trip already arriving from Berlin.

Ireland's Prime Minister Micheál Martin welcomed Burnham's appointment, saying he hoped to work with him to strengthen ties between the U.K., Ireland and the European Union.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Britain and Germany remained "close allies and partners," and invited Burnham to visit Berlin.

But Burnham is likely to face some of the same challenges that stymied Starmer: rising costs of living, slow growth and that volatile American ally across the Atlantic.

World.title: Trump tells Carney to take action on wildfire smoke during World Cup chat
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. U.S. President Donald Trump personally told Prime Minister Mark Carney to stop poisoning American air and take action to put out wildfires burning across the country. Trump said he raised the issue of wildfire management with Carney when the two leaders appeared together to watch the World Cup Final between Argentina and Spain in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sunday. "I told him, I mean, 'You got to stop these fires from coming in and, you know, poisoning our air. Our air has been poisoned,'" Trump said at Joint Base Andrews after the game. The U.S. president said he has a "good relationship" with Carney before reiterating his threat to impose financial penalties on his northern neighbour for the wildfires' impact on U.S. air quality. "If we can help them, we'll help them. But maybe they should pay some damages or something, or we should do some tariffs. But it was terrible," Trump said. "I mean you had businesses closing in particular Michigan." Cities in the state shut down beaches, splash pads, the Red Oaks water park and even indoor pools because of the toxic smoke that blanketed Michigan and other northern U.S. states. The Detroit Free Press reported that dozens of workers at Ford's Michigan assembly plant were taken to hospital after inhaling wildfire smoke inside non-air-conditioned plants. Trump's threats over wildfires Trump first threatened to make Canada pay for the cost of U.S. air quality in a Friday social media post when he joined some Republican House representatives' broad criticism of Canada's forest management practices calling them "wilful negligence." "We are holding Canada responsible for the fact that they are not properly maintaining their Forests, and brush therein, and the United States is being unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted, and unhealthy air," the president wrote in a social media post on Friday. "This is Willful Negligence, and becoming a yearly occurrence, costing the United States Billions of Dollars, which cost of this pollution must of necessity be added to the TARIFFS Canada is currently paying." This morning, I met with federal workers in Ottawa who are supporting the wildfire response efforts in Northwestern Ontario and across the country. This is one of the most intense wildfire seasons in Canadian history due to extreme heat waves and record-breaking dry conditions.… pic.twitter.com/ubS7Gupgam —MarkJCarney During a wildfire briefing in Toronto on Monday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford described Trump's comments as "disappointing to say the least." "With all the assets the U.S. has, he's sitting there complaining," Ford said. "Why don't you send up some water bombers? Why don't you start helping us, like we would help you in a heartbeat? "You should support your neighbours. That's my message to the president." On Friday, Ford reminded the U.S. president, and other Republican legislators, it was time to repay the efforts Canada undertook to restore electricity in the U.S. after Hurricane Helene in 2024 and the California wildfires last year. "If there's some politicians out there chirping away, well maybe what you should do rather than complain is send support, send help, because we have done the exact same thing for our American friends. That's what you're supposed to do," Ford said at the time. During his remarks on Friday in Toronto, Ford said he thinks Americans are good neighbours but need to start acting that way.

World.title: Canada's inflation rate eased to 2.8% in June thanks to lower gas prices
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's inflation rate eased to 2.8 per cent in June as gas prices decelerated during the month, Statistics Canada data showed Monday.

Higher oil prices due to the war between the U.S. and Iran have sent the cost of gas up in recent months and helped pull the inflation rate higher in May to 3.2 per cent.

The ceasefire and diplomatic talks last month helped ease oil prices, leading to a 10.2 per cent drop in the cost of gas month-over-month.

Since then, tensions have risen after the memorandum of understanding between the countries collapsed, and pump prices have climbed again as a result.

Statistics Canada says inflation was unchanged from May to June when gas prices are taken out of the equation.

Price hikes at the grocery store also eased to 3.9 per cent in June, down from 4.3 per cent in May.

Costs for fresh fruit grew at a slower pace, according to the data agency, especially for grapes. But prices for some grocery items accelerated — like fresh or frozen chicken, which rose by 5.7 per cent, and bread, rolls and buns, which were up six per cent.

Prices for travel-related expenses also surged as the World Cup kicked off. The cost of traveller accommodation was up around 20 per cent year-over-year in Ontario and British Columbia — mainly in host cities Toronto and Vancouver — last month.

Air transportation costs also rose 9.6 per cent annually due to higher jet fuel prices and increased domestic travel demand, Statistics Canada said, marking the largest increase since February 2023.

BMO Economics managing director Benjamin Reitzes noted that core measures of inflation that strip out more volatile metrics were lower than expected.

"While headline inflation remains above target, underlying pressures are subdued and slowing," Reitzes wrote in a note to investors. Given that, he expects the Bank of Canada to stay "comfortably on the sidelines" for the rest of the year.

Last week, the central bank left its key lending rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent. The central bank signalled at the time that there were few signs that price pressures from the Iran war were spilling over into broader inflation.

World.title: Alberta municipalities can’t campaign for or against separatism. Here's why
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Alberta’s fall referendum approaches, the province’s cities and towns have been told they can’t campaign on the issues.

Elected officials have been expressing opinions on Alberta independence and in turn, urging residents to vote one way or another in the referendum in October.

Last week, Edmonton city council backed Mayor Andrew Knack’s motion “that the City of Edmonton declare that Edmonton and Alberta are a vital part of Canada, and that Alberta should remain a province within a united Canada.”

Knack told CBC News on Wednesday that council is responsible for representing the city and that he thinks the referendum question is a distraction.

“If Edmonton were to separate from Canada, there would be significant economic harm,” Knack said.

“I have to spend time now reassuring potential employers, talking to investors who are asking the question of me, ‘should I invest in here with all of this that's going on right now?’ “

While mayors and councillors are allowed to take a position, Elections Alberta legislation dictates that municipalities aren’t permitted to raise money or advertise to support a side.

WATCH | Referendum rules for elected officials: What can elected officials say about the fall referendum? There are some rules | Duration 2:09 Many elected officials across Alberta are not hiding their feelings about the fall referendum, but there is a fine line about how far they can go. The CBC’s Nicole Healey has more on what rules officials have to follow.

Under the Elections Finances and Contributions Act, municipalities are considered prohibited corporations and not allowed to be a third-party advertiser, which means they can't take in or spend over $1,000.

Brendan Boyd, a MacEwan University political science professor, said that politicians can give their opinions but have to be careful about what may be considered advertising or campaigning.

"Of course they can say things and pass motions, as the City of Edmonton did,” Boyd said in an interview Wednesday.

Advertising and campaigning, he said, could include things like attending and speaking at events.

”They have to be pretty careful with how much they do and what exactly they do if they want to be supportive of one position or another."

Calgary Mayor Jeremy Farkas has taken a strong stance against separation.

“We have to stand up, we have to fight and we need to push back,’ Farkas told CBC News last week.

“So I'm going to be doing more than just moral support. I think that given the economic carnage that separation would incur on the city of Calgary specifically, we have a duty and responsibility to act.”

Farkas is calling on the provincial government and the premier to change the legislation to allow municipalities to formally campaign.

But Calgary Coun. Landon Johnson said in an interview earlier this month he thinks cities and towns can help ensure everything goes smoothly for the referendum, but he doesn't think they should be picking sides.

"There's elected officials and then there's bureaucrats. And so for me, the bureaucrat side is supposed to be as neutral as possible on as many things as possible," he said.

Last week, Elections Alberta posted a bulletin aiming to clarify the rules for municipalities under the Elections Finances and Contributions Act.

“In response to much confusion and misinformation about what qualifies as referendum advertising under the EFCDA, as well as many questions and complaints to my office, this Interpretation Bulletin helps political participants and electors understand and comply with the legislation,” wrote Gordon McClure, chief electoral officer

“This also demonstrates my office’s commitment to the fair and impartial administration of electoral legislation and holding all political participants equally accountable.”

Confusing the issue slightly, according to Boyd, is that the same rules apply to the 10-question referendum as they do with general elections, when municipalities aren’t allowed to campaign in support of specific parties.

“It's because it's a referendum and there's a specific question, there needs to be clarity around what is just talking generally good or bad about Canada or Alberta and what is actually advertising,” Boyd said.

World.title: Andy Burnham becomes Britain's 7th PM in the past decade
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Andy Burnham, speaking outside 10 Downing Street on Monday, says he's 'acutely conscious' that he's the seventh prime minister of the United Kingdom since 2016. 'We will make this moment a circuit-breaker for Britain.'

Britain needs to show the world it can regain stability, new PM says

Andy Burnham became the fifth British prime minister in four years and the seventh in a decade as he formally accepted an invitation from King Charles to form a government.

The meeting quickly followed on the heels of Keir Starmer offering his resignation.

Burnham secured nominations from 379 of the 403 Labour lawmakers in the House of Commons to officially became leader of the Labour Party last week.

Britain's parliamentary democracy allows governing parties to change leaders, and thus prime ministers, without the need for a general election. The next national election doesn't have to be held until 2029.

In his first speech as prime minister, Burnham said he hoped to be a "circuit breaker" to end the trend of instability in British politics.

"Britain ⁠needs to show the world that we ‌can regain our stability once again," Burnham said outside ⁠10 Downing Street.

"We have ⁠not been good ⁠enough, ⁠and ​we need to be ​better."

King Charles welcomes Andy Burnham, left, during an audience at Buckingham Palace in London on Monday, where he invited the leader of the Labour Party to become prime minister and form a new government. (Aaron Chown/Reuters)

In ​a clip recorded before he was officially appointed as British ​leader but released after his ⁠speech in ⁠Downing Street, Burnham ‌said that among his first telephone calls internationally would be U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"President Zelenskyy will be ⁠left ⁠in ​no doubt whatsoever that Britain's support is steadfast, ​it is ⁠resolute. It will be there for him, and I will be there for him personally, too," Burnham told reporters.

Zelenskyy was among a number of world leaders to offer congratulations to Burnham on social media, a list that included Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"I look forward to working with Prime Minister Burnham to build greater security, stability and prosperity on both sides of the Atlantic," said Carney.

With respect to Washington, Burnham's predecessor ingratiated himself with Trump for more than a year, only for the U.S. president to later express frustration over what he perceived as Starmer's lack of support for the Iran war. When Starmer announced his plans to resign weeks ago, Trump described him as a "lovely man" and a "sort of friend of mine."

Immediate economic challenges

While Burnham has been regarded as one of the Labour Party's best communicators, he faces many of the same problems as his predecessor, including a sluggish economy, a cost-of-living squeeze fuelled by wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and overstretched public services.

Promising Britons "some ⁠breathing space now," he said on Monday that the government would set out some measures to tackle ‌the high cost of living, and how it plans to fund them.

While wishing Burnham "every success," Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch of the Conservative Party touched on the hard choices the new prime minister faced, in a social media post.

WATCH | Burnham's remarkable turn in fortunes, and challenges he faces: How Andy Burnham went from Manchester mayor to U.K. PM | Duration 5:40 Andy Burnham is set to become U.K. prime minister following Keir Starmer’s resignation. For The National, CBC’s Chris Brown breaks down how the former Greater Manchester mayor won over voters and asks: is it enough to fix a fractured Britain?

"Every announcement he makes should be properly funded," she said. "We cannot borrow more money and the tax burden is already too high, so the only answer is spending cuts."

Burnham was born in Liverpool, where his father worked as a telephone engineer and his mother as a receptionist. He graduated in English from Cambridge, where he met his wife — Marie-France van Heel, a Dutch-born, Belgian-raised marketing professional known to friends as "Frankie." The couple have three children.

He is not a stranger to federal politics, having first served as MP beginning in 2001 when Tony Blair was prime minister, and later as culture and then health minister under Blair's successor, Gordon Brown.

Burnham mounted unsuccessful bids for the Labour leadership in 2010 and 2015.

Farage calls for election

Labour regularly trails behind anti-immigration party Reform UK in opinion polls, with an election due no later than 2029. Labour suffered disastrous results in local elections in May, triggering pressure on Starmer to step down that he couldn't resist.

Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage called for an immediate election.

"Andy Burnham cannot be allowed to make the 'biggest changes in politics for 40 years' without a mandate," he said.

Keir Starmer speaks as he leaves 10 Downing Street. (Kirsty Wigglesworth/The Associated Press)

Starmer made his farewell speech outside 10 Downing Street before meeting with the king to tender his resignation. He told supporters that "my work is done" and that he was leaving with "good grace" and a "smile."

"I wish him every success," he said of Burnham.

Starmer led Labour a mid-2024 election rout as the party more than doubled its seats from a loss five years earlier, even as its share of the total vote only went up by about two percentage points. Starmer's two years in office marred by missteps and judgment errors that eroded his standing with his party and the public.

Starmer is staying on as MP of Holborn and St. Pancras.

World.title: Young people grew up in the digital age. So why do they love movies on film?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Jaime Rebanal has dedicated much of his life to analog film. He attends nearly every celluloid movie screening he can find in Toronto — sometimes watching several a day.

Rebanal, a filmmaker himself, is 27 — meaning that when he was growing up, Hollywood was already dominated by digital technology. Even so, he says he has been "enraptured" by film.

"When you're seeing something on film, there's a lot of fine details that you don't get digitally," he said at an event at the Toronto International Film Festival's (TIFF) Lightbox in Toronto about film formats. The event was held as part of a retrospective on director Christopher Nolan, ahead of the release of his newest film The Odyssey. It even featured a large Imax camera that presenters noted was Nolan's favourite.

Young people are often stereotyped as phone-addicted shut-ins who won't date , drink , read books or have kids . Yet some of them are behind an analog film renaissance at movie theatres, as they look for immersive, community-focused experiences you can't get online or at home.

And Imax, known for its towering screens and enveloping audio, is perhaps the best exampl e of this. The Odyssey is the first narrative feature shot entirely on 70-mm Imax film.

"They know about the brand and they know the brand means quality," said Mark Welton, global president at Imax Theatres. "So, you know, we're seeing tons of demand [from] young people."

The audience knows what it wants

The entertainment industry was hard hit by the COVID-19 pandemic and the actors' and writers' strikes after that, leaving executives scrambling to lure audiences back into theatres.

Young people are at the forefront of that resurgence: 85 per cent of Canadians under 35 are moviegoers, according to a 2025 Telefilm Canada report , compared to 54 per cent of those 35 and up. Meanwhile, just 12 per cent of the population accounted for half of all admissions, meaning more viewers were repeat customers.

That's true for analog film screenings, as well. When TIFF showed a 70-mm screening of Top Gun, a third of the audience was under 25, a spokesperson said. For recent showings of 2001: A Space Odyssey and Vertigo, the figure sat at just under 30 per cent.

"Gen-Z … are into the materiality of media, because they grew up, you know, watching films on their phones," said Janine Marchessault, a professor at York University who led a research project into the early history of Imax.

"This new generation are really interested in the capabilities of film as a medium."

Much of the film industry shifted to shooting and projecting movies digitally because doing so is cheaper and more forgiving than analog film. But the resolution of large-format film still outperforms most digital cameras.

Unlike digital, analog film is made up of crystals rather than pixels, which is what creates its characteristic grain. This can be simulated digitally — but on celluloid, the grain pattern is unique to each shot.

WATCH | From the CBC Archives | What were young people of the 1970s into? The '40s: Nostalgia for the '40s in 1974 | Duration 2:19 Young people are exploring the fashions, movies and especially the music of the 1940s.

Marchessault believes there is a bifurcated audience for analog film: the boomers who recognize its value from growing up with it, as well as a new group of young people, who have independently learned to appreciate the medium.

"There's a whole cinephile culture that's been going up for a while," she said. "There's an audience that is now demanding beautiful images, high resolution, good sound."

TIFF has noticed a similar trend, said its chief programming officer, Anita Lee.

"Often, independent arthouse cinema is outperforming our more commercial, theatrical releases."

A person looks at two frames of film strips. (Hanna Lee/CBC)

Meanwhile, the communal aspect of watching a movie is a big draw for a cohort whose adolescence was defined by lockdowns and physical isolation.

"I do really feel like this is all part of a similar kind of desire again for material reality and wanting to experience something that feels authentic," she said.

Viral knowledge

Imax's Welton credits social media with teaching young people technical knowledge — like, say, how to differentiate between 70-mm and 35-mm screenings, where the former is much larger and has higher resolution compared to the latter's standard aspect ratio.

He cited director Ryan Coogler as an example, who while promoting his film Sinners last year, released a video explaining the different film formats and their aspect ratios. It might seem like industry jargon, but the clip garnered more than one million views on YouTube.

WATCH | Ryan Coogler explains aspect ratios:

"I think there's just a lot more information out there for young people to understand it," said Welton. "And they make it very understandable … when it's on social media."

Coogler's video was a big part of how Govind Chandak, 25, became interested in the medium.

He was curious why a director would seek it out, given its expense. He then saw Paul Thomas Anderson's One Battle After Another on 70-mm Imax, which he described as "probably the best film presentation I've ever seen."

Now, he's part of a movie club on the messaging platform Discord that he says has some 1,000 members. Many of them regularly meet up to watch and discuss films. For The Odyssey, a segment of the group co-ordinated to buy tickets at the exact same time.

"Honestly, I'm just someone that appreciates visual quality quite a lot," said Chandak, after the film event in Toronto. "So for me, watching that ... resolution at the Imax theatre is, I don't know.

"I can't explain it; you have to go in."

The Imax MSM 9802 camera, said to be director Christopher Nolan's favourite, is seen on stage. (Hanna Lee/CBC)

Many people — even those well versed in the technical aspects — who spoke to CBC News described analog film with near-mystical reverence.

One presenter at the TIFF event noted: "A comparison that kind of stuck with me once was … digital is the way you sort of experience reality, but film is the way you remember it."

At the end of the talk, particularly keen attendees crowded the stage to speak with the presenters. But the Nolan-favoured Imax camera proved just as popular, as people gathered in throngs to get a closer look at the device.

Some pulled out their phones, flipped the camera and took a selfie with it.

World.title: What did Vancouver get from the World Cup?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For five weeks, Vancouver felt different.

The FIFA Men's World Cup brought packed fan zones, busy transit and a jolt of public energy to Vancouver — a place often dubbed “No Fun City.”

From the stands to the streets, fans were loud and visible.

But the legacy of a major event is measured by more than crowds and noise. Observers say it also depends on the public cost, the effect on businesses and residents, and whether the excitement around soccer can turn into something more permanent.

Now that Vancouver’s time as a host city is over, the city is starting to weigh what the event meant — and what, if anything, will last.

Vancouver showed up

The city hosted seven matches at B.C. Place during the tournament from June 13 to July 7. Despite concerns over ticket prices , FIFA said each game was a full house, with 52,497 fans in attendance — more than 367,000 spectators in total.

Team Canada fans cheer during a group stage match between Canada and Qatar during the FIFA Men's World Cup in Vancouver on Thursday, June 18, 2026. (Maggie MacPherson/CBC)

Outside B.C. Place, fans gathered at public viewing sites across the region. The Vancouver host committee reported more than half a million visits at the FIFA Fan Festival at Hastings Park. In North Vancouver, the city said more than 340,000 people attended Canada House at the Shipyards.

TransLink said Vancouver’s seven match days added an average of 87,000 extra transit boardings per day across the region. The busiest day came June 24, when Canada played Switzerland at B.C. Place. That day, the system recorded nearly 1.4 million boardings, with TransLink calling this its highest ridership day in more than six years.

In an interview on the CBC’s The Early Edition, Vancouver Deputy Mayor Sarah Kirby-Yung said the crowds were about more than soccer enthusiasm.

“Everybody became so Canadian… It was like Canada Day every day," she said. “That pride in our city was something that I can’t remember feeling anything exactly like before."

Fans watch as Canada plays Bosnia and Herzegovina during the FIFA World Cup at Canada Soccer House in North Vancouver, B.C., on Friday June 12, 2026. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

Vancouver’s setup also earned outside praise. In June, Sports Illustrated ranked Vancouver first among the 16 World Cup host cities, citing its transit, walkability, mild weather and B.C. Place’s downtown location.

Can Granville Street keep the energy?

At a special council meeting on July 2, Vancouver Mayor Ken Sim said the city needed to build on what he called the “outstanding success” of Granville Street’s pedestrian pilot during the World Cup.

During the tournament, five blocks of Granville Street were turned into a pedestrian zone between West Georgia and Davie streets. It was created for the World Cup, but city council has voted to extend the closure until Sept. 7.

Canada soccer fans on Granville Street, Vancouver, before the FIFA World Cup match between Canada and Qatar at B.C. Place on June 18, 2026. (Jan Zeschky/CBC)

The Downtown Vancouver Business Improvement Association (DVBIA) has been given up to $1.25 million to help program and animate the street, with any unspent money returned to the city. The extension is expected to cost up to $4.75 million, including the cost of sanitation, traffic management and policing.

Kirby-Yung said this move gives the city a chance to see what works after the World Cup.

“Think of something like Gastown,” she said. “You’ve got buskers, you’ve got patios, you’ve got restaurants, you’ve got cafes and you’ve got something for people to do.”

But the area faces a deeper challenge. A planning document from the DVBIA says approximately one-in-four storefronts on the street is vacant, with “longstanding social challenges affecting the corridor.”

The document says “simply removing vehicles is not enough.” It says the extension needs programming that gives people a reason to visit, stay longer and support local businesses.

Canada soccer fans on Granville Street, Vancouver, before the the FIFA World Cup match between Canada and Qatar at B.C. Place on June 18, 2026. (Jan Zeschky/CBC)

Programming is expected to evolve week to week during the extension, with live music, interactive games, pop-up markets and patios showing sports. Some activations will also be tied to special dates and community celebrations, including a National Day of the Cowboy event with country music on July 25.

Beyond Granville Street, city officials said the tournament’s legacy will be reflected in improvements at B.C. Place, modern infrastructure and field lighting at Killarney Park, and exposure for the PNE’s new 10,000-capacity amphitheatre.

Legacy for who?

Before the World Cup, some advocates warned about the impact the event could have on Vancouver’s unhoused population.

Fears about displacement were raised as governments anticipated spending heavily on security for the tournament. In figures updated in June, the province estimated combined local and provincial safety and security costs for Vancouver’s World Cup at about $242 million, partially offset by $100 million in federal funding.

Fiona York, a local advocate for unhoused individuals, said she noticed a stronger police presence downtown and more pressure on people to move their belongings.

“People were being asked… not only to just put their tents down flat, but to pack them up and take them away,” she said. “So it's a little bit more dramatic, a little more severe.”

York also questioned whether the tournament would leave any lasting benefits for vulnerable people.

“We've got Granville continuing this pedestrian zone, all those millions going into that. Was there not something that could be done for the Downtown Eastside if there was money to be spared?”

York said any discussion of legacy should include funding for basic needs in the Downtown Eastside, including washrooms, facilities and housing.

In May, the City of Vancouver released its final human rights action plan for the World Cup. The city also said homelessness services and outreach programs would continue throughout the tournament.

Can World Cup excitement grow the game?

B.C. Soccer CEO Gabriel Assis said the World Cup created a rare opportunity to grow the sport in the province.

“Our focus is to ensure that the momentum of the FIFA World Cup 2026 becomes more than a moment,” Assis said. “We want it to become a movement.”

He said the province already has more than 150,000 soccer participants and more than 100 soccer organizations. And while the tournament has helped “accelerate interest” in the game, he said B.C. will need more investment in fields, coaches and match officials to keep up with demand.

Assis pointed to several projects already underway, including Canada’s first FIFA Arena in Langley, a FIFA26 50/50 funding program, 20 mini-pitches planned across B.C. and a new provincial field inventory to track supply and demand.

Going forward, Assis said the goal is to create a “legacy of improved facilities, stronger programs, and increased access to the game.”

Kids are pictured playing soccer at the Cloverdale Athletic Park in Surrey. Soccer clubs in both Surrey and North Vancouver are calling on their cities to build more turf fields. (CBC)

Jeff Clarke, a former Canadian national team player and senior technical director for Surrey United Soccer Club, said he hopes the tournament helps attract more young players and keep teens in the sport longer. But he added Canada needs more playing opportunities and lower costs for families.

“If you lean too heavily on the participant, then the entry fees are too high and that's a barrier,” Clarke said.

According to Clarke, entry-level programs at Surrey United cost about $100 a month, while higher-level teams can cost families several times that, plus travel and transportation.

What remains after the crowds?

The Parliamentary Budget Officer estimated public spending tied to Vancouver’s host-city costs at $578 million.

The province, meanwhile, has projected the tournament would generate long-term economic benefits, including about $1 billion in GDP for B.C. during the World Cup and in the five years that follow.

While the final accounting is still to come, the legacy of Vancouver’s experience as a host city will be measured by more than numbers. It will depend on what happens next: on Granville Street, in the Downtown Eastside, and on the fields where the next generation of soccer athletes will play.

World.title: She needs $12K-a-month drug to treat incurable cancer, but insurance won’t pay
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Sophie Djeme-Mi Koumazock, 43, was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer in May 2025. When the oral medication she was taking stopped working, her doctor suggested an alternative – but her insurer, Canada Life, won't cover the cost.

‘I want to live’: Quebec mother with Stage 4 cancer fights insurance for $12K-a-month drug

When 43-year-old Sophie Djeme-Mi Koumazock was told her incurable metastatic breast cancer was no longer responding to her medication, she was reassured knowing she had another option.

Her doctor said her profile made her a candidate for the drug Truqab. While it wouldn’t cure her, it would give the Quebec City mother of four young kids more time with her family.

But her hope didn’t last long.

Costing up to $12,000 a month — double her previous medication that had been covered by her insurer Canada Life — Djeme-Mi Koumazock was shocked to learn she wouldn’t be reimbursed for the new treatment.

“It’s destroyed me. I didn’t know what to do,” she said.

While Quebec's health insurance board covers Truqap under exceptional circumstances, federal public servant Djeme-Mi Koumazock is enrolled in the Public Service Health Care Plan (PSHCP). Administered by Canada Life, the federal plan does not cover the drug.

Djeme-Mi Koumazock contacted her employer and union. While her union is helping her with her case, she's been told the decision is policy. She's now forced to pay out of pocket until she finds a solution.

“I need this medication to survive, I never would have thought they would hit me with a no,” she said. “I want to live.”

Djeme-Mi Koumazock pictured with her partner, Jonathan Tekeu, and their four kids aged three, six, 12 and 13. (Bruno Giguère/Radio-Canada)

Gap in coverage

In its refusal letter sent to Djeme-Mi Koumazock on June 19 and reviewed by CBC News, Canada Life wrote its program requires the review of “factors such as [the drug’s] efficacy, safety, and cost effectiveness.”

It said following a review conducted by “qualified health-care professionals at Canada Life,” the PSHCP Prior Authorization Program determined the drug is excluded from coverage.

In an emailed statement to CBC News, Canada Life said as plan sponsor, the Government of Canada determines what is covered under its benefits plan.

This includes any differences from what may be covered under Quebec’s health insurance board, the Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ).

Djeme-Mi Koumazock is now waiting for a response from Beneva — her partner’s insurer — to which she has now been added as a beneficiary. She's hoping they will help foot the bill. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)

In an emailed statement, a representative for the Treasury Board of Canada, which manages PSHCP policy, says the optional health-care plan offered to eligible public service employees, pensioners and dependants is designed to supplement provincial and territorial health insurance plans.

But it says the PSHCP is not required to provide the same basic coverage as RAMQ.

The Treasury Board confirmed Truqap is not an eligible prescription drug under its PSHCP prior authorization program.

But Djeme-Mi Koumazock doesn’t understand why this gap exists. She calls it “inequity.”

“Why, between two Quebecers, could one have access to this medication and not me?” she asked.

Woman’s oncologist wants to give her time

Djeme-Mi Koumazock’s oncologist, Dr. Brigitte Poirier, says Truqap is a good option for her patient and that the efficacy of this treatment is proven by the literature.

Poirier, a surgical oncologist at CHU de Québec-Université Laval and head of its breast cancer centre, says it’s about controlling the disease the best they can.

“When the medication we are giving stops [working] … and we lose the control, we have to change the treatment,” she said. “It’s the thing we have to do now.”

Djeme-Mi Koumazock’s oncologist, Dr. Brigitte Poirier, says she wants to control the disease the best they can. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)

While there are other options for Djeme-Mi Koumazock, including chemotherapy and other anti-hormonal medications, “we want the best for our patients,” Poirier said.

“It’s not easy for someone [who is] like 43 years old with young kids. We want to give them time.”

Djeme-Mi Koumazock wants that too. It’s part of why she and her partner decided to temporarily dip into their savings — and retirement fund, if necessary — so she can start the treatment as soon as it is available.

Djeme-Mi Koumazock is now waiting for a response from Beneva — her partner’s insurer — to which she has now been added as a beneficiary.

In an emailed statement from Beneva, it confirmed Truqap is part of its standard plan, since it applies the criteria established by RAMQ — therefore counting the medication as an exceptional drug.

‘Very unlikely’ 2 insurers refuse coverage, says RAMQ

Djeme-Mi Koumazock has called RAMQ numerous times and spoken with agents to request that the provincial agency step in.

CBC News asked RAMQ if it would cover the cost of the medication if her partner’s insurance also refuses to pay.

In an emailed statement, RAMQ did not answer if it would cover the medication, but pointed to the fact that private insurance, provided through an individual’s partner, should be able to cover costs.

“It’s very unlikely that two different insurers refuse to reimburse a medication that RAMQ would accept to cover and, to our knowledge, a situation of this kind has never been brought to our attention,” read the statement.

Same problem for another Quebec woman

The process to get medication covered took Nathalie Samson from Saint-Philippe, Que., months when she was in the same situation as Djeme-Mi Koumazock earlier this year.

Diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer in 2022, she had been on medication for years in an effort to stop the progression of the Stage 4 disease.

But this past December, her body stopped responding and her care team referred her to try the drug Truqap.

“This is when the battle started,” said Michel Boulay, Samson’s partner.

“She experienced a lot of stress, she was sick. This lasted four and a half months.”

Nathalie Samson and her partner, Michel Boulay, from Saint-Philippe, Que., went through a similar ordeal earlier this year. (Submitted by Nathalie Samson)

As a federal employee, Samson was also denied coverage under the Canada Life plan.

Boulay requested Samson be brought onto his work insurance plan with Manulife in February. She was able to get coverage for Truqap through Manulife and AstraZeneca — the drug manufacturer.

Around March, Samson's cancer began to stabilize while she was still taking her old medication. But if things worsen, she says she now has the ability to start taking the new drug.

Samson spoke to the media about the ordeal in the spring and says she doesn’t “want this to happen to someone else.”

“I’m very happy that someone else is coming forward and taking charge because there will be others,” she said.

The long claim process

In situations where insured clients’ claims are refused, Patrick Martin-Ménard, a medical attorney, said people should exercise their right to a review request.

While he has not analyzed either of the women’s cases, he noted that contesting the refusal of a claim or even hiring a lawyer or expert for a case can be a lengthy process.

“Obviously, patients are already dealing with significant health issues and all the challenges that come with it. And then they have to add this battle on top of that,” he said.

“I think that is certainly a consideration that insurance companies should have when making this type of decision.”

Djeme-Mi Koumazock calls the gap in coverage ‘inequity.’ (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)

Djeme-Mi Koumazock doesn’t want to put fault on her insurer, but is just trying to get the case settled as fast as possible for both her and her family’s sake.

“I have the right to get answers,” she said.

“These steps are long and I don’t have a lot of time.”

World.title: Government tip-off prompted spy agency to look into federal scientist, CSIS says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The country's top spy agency says Natural Resources Canada approached it with concerns about former federal scientist Dennis Lu more than two decades ago, not the other way around — and has made a rare disclosure of one of its documents in court to set the record straight, CBC News has learned.

There are also new details about part of the reason for a 23-month delay between the last Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) briefing about Lu to his employer in February 2021 and the start of Natural Resources' internal investigation into Lu in January 2023.

Lu's security clearance was eventually revoked and an RCMP investigation resulted in criminal charges of breach of trust and unauthorized use of a computer.

It's alleged that he used his access to the Natural Resources network to copy a total of more than 2,500 documents onto a USB key and external drive.

He faces trial in Ottawa's Superior Court by a judge alone in January.

This spring, a Department of Justice lawyer addressed court on behalf of CSIS "just to clarify" how the entire file on Lu began more than two decades ago.

"It wasn't CSIS flags per se, it was a government tip-off," Sheldon Leung said.

The lawyer's comments came during a pre-trial motion brought by Lu's defence team in its fight to access to hundreds of pages of third-party records that it said were relevant to the case — access it won for most of the documents.

Hosted Chinese delegation

Leung then read part of a CSIS document that the spy agency wanted the judge to see, dated Nov. 20, 2000 — the same year as CSIS's first briefing to Natural Resources about Lu.

"On Nov. 14, 2000, a source provided the following unsolicited information regarding a visiting delegation. According to source one, Mr. Dennis Lu, research scientist at [Natural Resources'] Advanced Combustion Technology branch (ACT), had invited a visiting Chinese delegation without the knowledge of his operational manager," the document reads.

"It was only after the fact, when questioned, that Lu provided the following information about the delegation to [his department's] security officials and his manager."

But Leung read no further, saying only that the rest of the CSIS document contained details about a meeting and some potentially sensitive government information.

This spring, a federal lawyer addressed court on behalf of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service 'just to clarify' how the entire file on Lu began more than two decades ago. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

'Resource constraints'

During a separate pre-trial motion brought by the defence this summer about whether the investigation breached Lu's privacy, Brad Lanthier, a former chief security officer at Natural Resources, testified about the team he first joined in November 2022, 21 months after the last CSIS briefing about Lu.

Under examination-in-chief by assistant Crown attorney Tim Radcliffe, Lanthier said the team had recently been separated from the IT department and wasn't set up to take a large investigation on.

"There were severe, I would say, resource constraints in terms of our ability to conduct anything more than traditional risk investigations at that point in time," said Lanthier, now the RCMP's director general of national communications.

"It took a little bit of time [before the investigation formally began in January 2023]," he said. "The security function was just kind of getting up and going."

Lanthier testified that soon after he arrived, he was briefed about Canada's Task Force on Science and National Security, whose "primary goal was to safeguard science and to protect it from intellectual property theft, with a focus on foreign actor interference."

'A significant amount of risk'

He also learned about the Chinese government's Thousand Talents Program, which aims to bring scientists and researchers from all over the world to China, as well as the country's intelligence law, which can be used to compel citizens to share information with China to benefit its national security and economy.

As for Lu, Lanthier was told by colleagues that CSIS had briefed Natural Resources about him multiple times, that he was taking an extended leave without pay in China, and that he had asked his supervisors for permission to teach in China.

Taken together with the foreign interference threats from China, Lanthier said he believed there was "a significant amount of risk." So he asked IT staff to search Lu's emails for specific keywords, with CSIS providing input on what the search terms would be.

Lu was not granted permission to teach in China, and his access to Natural Resources' network was cut off while he was on leave because there would have been no need for him to access it, Lanthier told court.

Lu's access to Natural Resources Canada's network was cut off while Lu was in China during his leave of absence ahead of retirement, court heard. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

Wrote MP to get network access back

Then Lu returned to Canada and asked for his network access to be reinstated — moves that were "surprising" to the federal department, Lanthier said, because Lu's original plan had been to transition into retirement during his leave in China.

Lu's request for network access was therefore denied, Lanthier said, and Lu's reaction to the denial raised further suspicions.

"I believe Mr. Lu used a few different avenues, including writing his MP, requesting his access back. At that point the risk [in my opinion] had escalated significantly given the travel, given the change in plans, and given the what appeared to be determined request to get access back," Lanthier testified.

We had no choice but to give him his [network] access back. - Brad Lanthier, former chief security officer for Natural Resources

"We were then informed that Mr. Lu had in fact amended his leave, so therefore, just like any employee, we had no choice but to give him his access back. But we did request [IT to conduct] daily activity reports [about] Mr. Lu."

He allegedly copied 2,414 documents off a Natural Resources shared server on July 7, 2023, and a further 188 documents on Aug. 9, 2023.

His security clearance was then revoked, Lanthier said.

Lanthier personally referred the case to the RCMP on Aug. 17, 2023. Based on "the sheer volume of files that had been transferred," Natural Resources then had to conduct a damage assessment to determine what was taken, whether it was of value, and whether other government departments would be affected, he said.

A USB key was one of two devices Lu allegedly used to copy Natural Resources documents off of the federal department's shared drive. (CBC)

Searched 16 years of emails, phone use

In cross-examination, Reem Zaia, one of Lu's defence lawyers, pointed out that many countries have talent programs, including Canada, and that Canada's Policy on Sensitive Technology Research and Affiliations of Concern came into effect in May 2024 — almost a year after the documents were allegedly copied.

Lanthier acknowledged no evidence was found that Lu was a member of China's Thousand Talents Program and said he didn't know exactly what CSIS's concerns about Lu were — aside from affiliations with the Chinese government — when the investigation into Lu was ordered and conducted.

Zaia also read aloud part of a document outlining the testimony Lanthier had been expected to give, which said that "the fact-finding review [into Lu] identified some associations and correspondence with individuals from a country of a concern [China], but it was not definitive based on the narrow search conducted at the time."

That "narrow search," as Zaia pointed out and Lanthier acknowledged, included 16 years of Lu's work emails — received, sent and/or deleted — from January 2007 to 2023. It also covered all communications to and from his work cellphone — calls, messages and/or texts — across the same 16 years.

No instructions to exclude Lu's private information were made, court heard.

Co-operative agreements with China

Lanthier also didn't dispute that:

Natural Resources security categorization standards allowed employees with security clearance such as Lu to store protected A-, B- and C-level documents on USB keys and external hard drives (A-level documents could cause injury to an individual, organization or government if compromised; B-level documents could cause serious injury; and C-level documents could cause extremely grave injury).

A report found that about 1,100 Natural Resources employees were using USB keys in 2023.

The standard operating procedure at Natural Resources allowed some staff 24/7 access to the federal department's network even if they had retired, according to a senior director of operations in an interview with RCMP. (Lanthier told Zaia he wasn't aware of that procedure, but had no reason to doubt it.)

He also wasn't aware that Natural Resources had a memorandum of understanding with China's National Energy Administration.

It took effect in June 2017, lasted five years, focused on energy, and "encouraged participants to promote technical and policy co-operation, including the exchange of experts and information as well as joint research," Zaia said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, back left, and Premier of China Li Qiang, back right, look on as Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson, front left, and Wang Hongzhi, Director of the National Energy Administration in China, front right, sign a memorandum of understanding to co-operate on energy in Beijing on Jan. 15, 2026. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

(There had been a previous memorandum between Natural Resources and China's National Energy Administration regarding nuclear energy in 2014. A new memorandum between the departments to strengthen energy co-operation took effect in January this year.)

Pre-trial motions in Lu's case are ongoing. Four weeks have been set aside for Lu's trial next year.

World.title: Hate has corrupted the world’s biggest charities: Full Comment podcast
World.content:
Article content

The Red Cross, Amnesty International, Doctors Without Borders, Human Rights Watch, UNICEF and more — they’re treated by governments and the media as neutral humanitarians working for everyone’s rights and welfare. But as Danielle Haas tells Brian, a new investigation by her organization EiGHT found them rife with bias, particularly against Jews and Israel. It uncovered charities refusing to acknowledge atrocities committed by Hamas, while ostracizing and even dismissing workers who dared speak up about human rights violations and blatant antisemitism, including within the organizations themselves. EiGHT, made up of former NGO leaders, is calling for transparency and oversight for charities whose discrimination goes largely unscrutinized, despite raking in billions of dollars in donations and funding. (Recorded July 17, 2026)

Heavy rain, strong winds, and snowfall expected as new frontal system approaches

SANTIAGO â Chile’s central and southern regions are preparing for a powerful frontal system bringing wind, rain, and snow over the coming days, according to updated forecasts from the DirecciÃ³n MeteorolÃ³gica de Chile (DMC). The system is expected to benefit water reserves, with substantial snowfall anticipated across the Andes from the Coquimbo to BiobÃ­o regions.

Alerts issued for high winds and snowfall

The DMC has issued weather alerts for much of central Chile due to moderate to strong winds and heavy precipitation. Gusts may exceed 80 km/h in areas from ValparaÃ­so to Ãuble, driven by a low-level jet stream. The strong winds may cause fallen branches, power outages, and “whiteout” conditions in mountainous regions.

Whiteout conditions occur when fresh, uncompacted snow is lifted and dispersed by strong winds, significantly reducing visibility.

Significant rainfall totals expected

: Heavier rainfall with up to 40 mm expected on Thursday. Maule, Ãuble, and BiobÃ­o Regions: Extended rainfall through Tuesday, June 17, with accumulations likely exceeding 100 mm during the holiday weekend.

Additionally, the DMC has warned of possible thunderstorms on Thursday in Maule, Ãuble, and BiobÃ­o due to post-frontal atmospheric instability, which may generate convective clouds with lightning.

Possible snowfall and sleet for Santiagoâs eastern sectors

The frontal system is accompanied by colder temperatures, increasing the likelihood of snow not only in the high mountains but also in lower pre-Andean areas closer to populated zones.

High likelihood of snow in San JosÃ© de Maipo, San FabiÃ¡n de Alico, Las Trancas, and Farellones.

These wintry conditions are welcomed by both residents and the tourism industry, as ski centers and mountain resorts benefit from fresh snowfall.

Cold snap to follow weekend storm

Once precipitation subsides, temperatures are expected to drop sharply starting Friday:

Santiago Metropolitan Region : Lows near 2Â°C, highs not exceeding 14Â°C.

: Lows near 2Â°C, highs not exceeding 14Â°C. ValparaÃ­so Coast : Minimums around 6Â°C, dropping to 1Â°C inland.

The cold spell could persist for several days, prompting authorities to advise residents to prepare appropriate clothing, ensure home heating, and prioritize care for vulnerable groups, including the elderly and young children.

Another frontal system possible Sunday

Meteorologists are closely monitoring the development of a second system forecast to impact central Chile on Sunday, June 15. Early estimates suggest additional rainfall of up to 40 mm for ValparaÃ­so and the Santiago Metropolitan Region, which may exacerbate soil saturation and pose travel disruptions if storms continue in quick succession.

The active weather pattern aligns with the seasonal transition into winter, marked by increased precipitation, colder temperatures, and more frequent snowfall across the Andes.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ð½ðððð¢ ððððððð (@nancysinatra)

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.
