World.title: More traffic headache coming for motorists in Liguanea
World.content:
Sewer upgrade work underway on Retreat Avenue off Old Hope Road on Saturday. The work will shortly be extended on Old Hope Road to its intersection with Wellington Drive. Naphtali Junior

MOTORISTS in the Liguanea area of St Andrew should brace for major traffic disruptions this summer as the National Water Commission (NWC) undertakes the renovation of sewage infrastructure along Old Hope Road

Speaking during a recent meeting of the Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s headquarters in St Andrew, Minister of Water Matthew Samuda said the work forms part of the Government’s ongoing programme to strengthen resilience through upgrading the county’s water and sewage network.

He explained that work on Munroe Road and Wellington Drive, which led to traffic snarls in the area for weeks, is now complete, allowing work to begin on the stretch of Old Hope Road that runs through Liguanea, Matilda’s Corner, and Seymour Avenue.

Samuda told Observer editors and reporters that work along that corridor was deliberately postponed to avoid disrupting students travelling to sit their various examinations.

“We didn’t start last month because we didn’t want to run the risk of a child being stuck in traffic trying to get to their PEP [Primary Exit Profile] exams at St Peter and Paul, or a child trying to get to Campion to do their CXC [Caribbean Examination Council] exams along that particular space. We expect to start in the coming week or so,” said the minister.

World.title: APOLOGY AND CORRECTION
World.content:
Dayton Campbell

On Monday, 13 July 2026, the Jamaica Observer published an article entitled ‘Dead girl’s ghost haunts Dayton’.

The Observer acknowledges that the headline was capable of conveying the false impression that Dr Campbell had some association with, or responsibility for, the rape and murder of Diane Smith. The Observer acknowledges that any such implication is entirely false.

Dr Campbell was an infant when Diane Smith was raped and murdered. He has never been implicated, suspected, or connected in any way with that tragic crime.

The Observer further acknowledges that Dr Campbell did not repeat or endorse any allegation connecting any person to the rape and murder of Diane Smith, whether debunked or otherwise.

The Jamaica Observer sincerely apologises to Dr Campbell for the distress, embarrassment, and reputational harm occasioned by the publication and withdraws any defamatory imputations arising therefrom.

World.title: Puzzling double murder in Mandeville
World.content:
An undated photo of murder victim Deneekia Pounall, 24, Knox Community College nursing student and resident of Heartease district in Manchester .

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Even as police here have launched a manhunt for a gunman who posed as a passenger in a taxi before disembarking the vehicle and killing two passengers on Saturday, detectives are struggling to make sense of the incident as up to press time they had not determined a motive for the attack.

“It is senseless…He paid his fare and got his change and the vehicle drove off and he just fired shots on it. The motive is not clear, because why would you shoot up a vehicle with seven people,” a senior police source told the Jamaica Observer on Sunday.

Police identified those killed as Deneekia Pounall, 24, a nursing student at Knox Community College, a resident of Heartease in the parish, and her neighbour 21-year-old Sadefa Henry.

According to the police, about 7:30 pm on Saturday, Pounall and Henry were seated in a Toyota Voxy operated as a public passenger vehicle on the Mandeville to Royal Flat route when a man, who was a passenger in the vehicle, disembarked at a section of Caledonia Road commonly referred to as Horseshoe Curve.

The man reportedly opened fire on the seven occupants of the taxi, hitting the two who were seated at the back of the vehicle.

They were taken to the Mandeville Regional Hospital where Pounall was pronounced dead on arrival, while Henry later succumbed to his injuries.

Residents of Heartease told the

Observer on Sunday that Pounall and Henry lived in neighbouring apartments at a property in the community.

“She was such a calm girl. She nuh talk, and the guy was quiet and humble, so this incident is quite puzzling,” said a resident who requested anonymity.

The double murder has increased the number of homicides reported in Manchester to 20 since the start of the year.

Just last week acting head of the police’s Area Three, Senior Superintendent Shane McCalla, predicted that fewer than 94 murders will be recorded across Manchester, Clarendon, and St Elizabeth by year end, following the launch of Operation Reset last month.

“We are trending upwards in the murder and aggravated assaults, so Operation Reset was primarily designed to address this…and in terms of the acquisitive crimes, we are trending down by 104. This is our commitment to the High Command that Area Three will deliver in December,” he told the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s High Command last Wednesday at the Mandeville police station.

McCalla gave a breakdown of murders statistics down the years in Area Three. He said in 2023 there were 189 murders, in 2024 there were 150 murders, while 94 murders were recorded last year.

“Year to date we have 58 [murders]. Despite seeing some issues where St Elizabeth is concerned… I am convinced and I am committing to you that we will end under the 94 [in December],” he vowed.

World.title: Sumfest history
World.content:
Mavado (left) and Vybz Kartel share the Sumfest stage. (Garfield Robinson)

For 18 years it remained one of dancehall’s biggest unanswered questions: Could the music that once divided a nation ever become the force that united it?

Shortly after 2:00 am on Sunday that question was answered inside Plantation Cove as a Taste of Reggae Sumfest delivered an experience of history-making proportions.

Vybz Kartel and Mavado stood shoulder to shoulder on the festival’s grand stage, writing a new chapter in one of the most defining narratives in dancehall culture. The showdown was far more than an exhibition of hit songs. It was the closing of a circle that began during the combative Gully/Gaza era — a rivalry that shaped an entire generation of dancehall fans and forever altered the genre’s landscape.

Dressed for battle, but performing in brotherhood, both deejays were ready to give fans exactly what they asked for.

Without hesitation, they reached back into the catalogue that made them icons. Serving up songs such as

The Real McKoy, Real Deal, Send A Hell, the entertainers elicited loud cheers of approval from the sold-out crowd.

The tension that once defined the rivalry had given way to celebration.

“This a history innu,” Mavado declared.

“Memba dat,” Kartel responded before embracing his long-time rival.

“We ago gi unnu supm unnu never see yet,” Kartel continued.

For two hours they spewed hit after hit from their arsenal of songs.

For Professor Donna Hope, one of Jamaica’s foremost authorities on dancehall culture, the significance of the moment extended well beyond nostalgia.

“Eighteen years later… We have been through many things, they’ve been in exile in different ways, they lost things, they gained things, and so the energy was different,” she reflected after the performance. “Gaza/Gully in 2008 was a very combative energy but Reggae Sumfest 2026, it was different. Their performance reminded people that dancehall culture is alive and well and Vybz Kartel and Mavado are powerful artistes that have matured and now understand the mission and are carrying it out.”

Even while revisiting songs born from lyrical warfare, the two men frequently completed each other’s lyrics, laughed together, and embraced the shared legacy they helped create. Records that once encouraged fans to choose sides became reminders of just how deeply both artistes have shaped modern dancehall.

Mavado confidently held his own with crowd favourites, including Weh Dem A Do, Top Shatta Nah Miss, Chat Too Much, Warn Dem, and Amazing Grace.

Kartel answered with equal force, unleashing anthem after anthem through Gaza Army, Broad Daylight, Kill Dem All, Done, Weh Dem A Go, Murder Informa, and Never Scared.

Female fans were delighted with selections including Love Dem, Picture Me & You, Beg You (A Touch), and Come Home, while Mavado countered with Squeeze Breast, Bicycle, Ever Blessed, When You Feel Lonely, and Never Believe You.

The surprises continued as Mavado invited Stacious to recreate their hit Come Into My Room, while Kartel called on Gaza Hindu to perform Spice’s verses on Ramping Shop and Virginity.

“It’s a good feeling to be back on a Sumfest stage,” said Stacious. “Tonight I’m here not just as an artiste, but as a fan of dancehall who lived through the era where Gully/Gaza did a run road… Mavado hasn’t performed in Jamaica for a while so I was happy to witness that return and be a part of it… [I]t’s always fun when we connect…” As they got ready to draw the curtains on their historic set, the clash songs and romance anthems gave way to messages of gratitude and faith as the deejays delivered Hope and Pray, God Is the Greatest, The Messiah, and Thank Yuh Jah. Then came the perfect ending. Their first collaboration, Happiest Days. “This a the first song me and him ever do,” Kartel reminded the audience. “Listen to it good and see how everything come full circle.” Few closing songs could carry greater symbolism — history, legacy secured!

World.title: Rastafari ganja rights review
World.content:
From left: Sancia Bennett Templer, permanent secretary, Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce; Delano Seiveright, minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce and chairman of the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce; Delroy Chuck, minister of justice and constitutional affairs; and Olivia “Babsy” Grange, minister of culture, gender, entertainment and sport, engage meeting attendees (out of picture) following Thursday’s high-level ministerial consultation on Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis framework at the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

THE Government on Thursday opened consultations on the country’s sacramental cannabis framework during a high-level policy meeting at the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

Justice Minister Delroy Chuck; Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia “Babsy” Grange; minister of state in the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Marisa Dalrymple-Philibert; and minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright led the talks with senior technocrats from the ministries.

The discussions were convened following recommendations of the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce, chaired by Seiveright, which identified the need for a coordinated consultation on policy and operational issues affecting Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis regime.

The meeting considered the existing legal and administrative framework with the objective of providing greater clarity, consistency, and certainty while safeguarding the religious freedoms provided under Section 7C(2)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act, which makes provision for members of the Rastafarian community to possess ganja.

The meeting discussed matters relating to the recognition and oversight of sacramental organisations, approved cultivation lands and spaces, cultivation and possession limits, transportation arrangements, enforcement protocols, and the need to clearly distinguish sacramental cannabis activities from Jamaica’s regulated, commercial cannabis industry.

Jamaica’s commercial cannabis industry is regulated exclusively by the Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) under the Dangerous Drugs Act and its Regulations, with no other entity having legal authority to license or regulate commercial cannabis activities.

There have been growing concerns surrounding the misuse of the sacramental framework to facilitate unlawful activities, as well as persistent confusion about what the law permits.

In recent times there have been repeated allegations from Rastafarians about facing prosecution over their use of ganja, despite the provision in law for its sacramental use.

Recently the

Jamaica Observer reported the case of Westmoreland resident Troy Harrison who had charges of possession of ganja and dealing in ganja against him dropped in the Westmoreland Parish Court.

The Crown offered no evidence on both charges on the basis that Harrison is a member of the Rastafarian community and therefore entitled to possess and use ganja for sacramental purposes.

“Some police continue to want to interpret the law how they want to,” attorney-at-law Marcus Goffe, who represented Harrison, told the

Observer.

“The Rastafari community is fed up with the continual targeting and unfair prosecution of members of the community for ganja, despite the 2015 amendments to the Dangerous Drugs Act intended to recognise and protect the community’s rights. It is clear that the narcotics police are not fully aware of the extent of Rastafari’s ganja rights or how they are to approach, investigate, determine, and resolve the rights of Rastafari in relation to ganja,” charged Goffe, who was then on a mission to have the seized ganja returned to Harrison.

Against charges such as the ones made by Goffe, the high-level meeting led by the Government ministers also explored mechanisms to strengthen coordination among the various ministries, the CLA, and the Jamaica Constabulary Force.

A significant part of the discussions focused on the possible transfer of responsibility for the operational governance and administration of sacramental cannabis matters to the Ministry of Culture, recognising the fundamentally religious and cultural character of the sacramental regime.

Ministers agreed that the proposal should form part of the ongoing consultation process as the Government works to strengthen governance; improve inter-ministerial coordination; and provide a clearer, more effective framework that protects legitimate sacramental rights while preserving public confidence, public safety, and the rule of law.

World.title: END OF THE ROAD
World.content:
Spain’s Rodri (left) and Argentina’s Lionel Messi fight for the ball during the World Cup football final match at the New York/New Jersey Stadium in East Rutherford, United States, on Sunday.

EAST RUTHERDORD, United States (AFP) — Ferran Torres scored a dramatic extra-time winner as Spain defeated holders Argentina 1-0 to win the World Cup on Sunday and shatter Lionel Messi’s dreams of a triumphant farewell to football’s greatest stage.

Barcelona striker Torres lashed home a thumping finish in the 106th minute to reward a dominant display by Spain against an Argentina team who failed to register a single shot on target in 120 minutes.

A star-studded crowd of 80,663 that included US President Donald Trump packed East Rutherford’s MetLife Stadium to see if Argentina captain, Messi, could crown his glittering career with a second World Cup victory.

But the 39-year-old maestro — almost certainly playing in his final World Cup game — was reduced to irrelevance as Spain took control early on against an Argentina team who committed cynical fouls throughout.

The South Americans’ skulduggery ended with midfielder Enzo Fernandez being sent off after a brutal challenge on Spain defender Pau Cubarsi in stoppage time.

For long periods, though, it looked as if Argentina may somehow hold on for a penalty shoot-out as Spain struggled to make the breakthrough.

But after Nico Williams had a goal controversially disallowed in extra time, Spain struck.

A lofted cross to the back post by Pedro Porro found Williams who nodded into the path of Torres to crash home the goal that clinched Spain’s second World Cup title after their maiden 2010 triumph.

“Ultimately, the goal belongs to 47 million people — not just me or the 26 players,” goal hero Torres said, referring to Spain’s approximate population.

“At the end of the day, all finals are tough; when you’re up against Messi, there’s a certain nervousness, but we always believed in our football and in ourselves.”

There were ugly scenes after the final whistle as Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes triggered a melee by grabbing Spain defender Eric Garcia around the throat in a skirmish that saw Spanish substitute Gavi thrown to the floor.

Messi, meanwhile, was seen with tears streaming down his face after receiving his runners-up medal in a ceremony headed by Trump — who was subjected to deafening boos and catcalls as he walked onto the pitch alongside FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

Trump and Infantino later presented the World Cup trophy to Spain Captain Rodri, the midfield general who had orchestrated La Roja’s superb win.

“We have won everything, and that is wonderful,” Spain Coach Luis de la Fuente said of his team. “They are a generation of footballers who are a source of pride for Spain.”

Before Sunday’s final, many pundits had predicted a technically inferior Argentina would seek to disrupt Spain’s smooth game with cynicism.

There was an early sign of the South Americans’ cynical game plan early on when Alexis Mac Allister went flying in with a studs-up challenge that struck Dani Olmo’s ankle.

Mac Allister escaped an early yellow card, although after Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic only awarded a foul.

Spain made their presence felt moments later, though, with Alex Baena poleaxing Messi with an elbow to the back that again escaped sanction.

Argentina continued to test referee Vincic’s patience with a series of niggly challenges, and Nicolas Tagliafico was lucky not to be cautioned after raking Lamine Yamal’s calf in a clumsy challenge.

Eventually, though, Vincic did reach for a yellow card, with Lisandro Martinez booked for a cynical challenge on Mikel Oyarzabal.

The final’s controversial half-time show featuring Madonna, Shakira, and Justin Bieber stretched to 27 minutes, but did little to upset Spain’s rhythm.

The Spanish piled on the pressure in a lopsided second half as Argentina hung on grimly.

De la Fuente sent on Pedri and Ferran Torres for Fabian Ruiz and Oyarzabal, and the chances continued with Argentina in full siege mode.

Pedri and Cubarsi both lashed long-range shots that Emi Martinez failed to grasp at the first attempt, but somehow Argentina continued to hold on.

The arrival of substitutes Williams and Mikel Merino gave fresh life to Spain’s attacking momentum, and the onslaught continued.

Fernandez’s reckless red card left Argentina down to 10 men heading into extra time.

Martinez had one last save deep in stoppage time when Yamal’s superb whipped free-kick was clawed wide.

The Spanish dominance continued in extra time. And it looked as if Spain had made the breakthrough when Williams slid a low finish into the net, but referee Vincic blew for a marginal foul on Nicolas Otamendi.

But the breakthrough came with Torres’ winner.

Argentina made a desperate last raid on Spain’s goal, but La Roja held firm to seal victory.

World.title: Nickeria Smickle
World.content:
Founder and chief executive officer of A-List Marketing & Entertainment Group Nickeria Smickle.

NICKERIA Smickle built a company, rebuilt communities after a hurricane, and now wants to prove that there’s more than one way to make it.

Ask Smickle for her formula and she won’t give you a business-school answer, instead she says, “faith, hunger, and a touch of delusion”.

It is a deceptively simple recipe for a woman who has spent the last six years proving that the most successful people are often the ones bold enough to begin before anyone else believes in them.

Smickle is the founder and chief executive officer of A-List Marketing & Entertainment Group and a 2026 Ignite Caribbean 30 Under 30 honouree in entrepreneurship and philanthropy.

But the title she is most interested in expanding isn’t her own. It’s the definition of success itself.

The instinct to give showed up early. At nine years old Smickle was selling candies at school and sharing her lunch money with classmates who had none. At 18, she rode the bus from Mandeville to Kingston to shoot photography at events and volunteer wherever she was needed. By 24 she was running a business and executing her own charity initiatives.

“My passion for service has always been at the core of my journey,” said Smickle.

Long before the company, that meant painting rooms for homeless women and children, joining community outreach, and showing up for beach clean-ups. The scale grew. The instinct never changed.

What sets Smickle apart is not just what she has built, but what she believes. Her argument is direct — not every child is meant to become a lawyer, teacher or doctor, and the ones who become musicians, painters, beauty professionals or entrepreneurs deserve to see their path celebrated too.

She is putting structure behind the belief. In late 2025, she registered the Anchor of Love JA Foundation in honour of her late mother. Its flagship project is Jamaica’s first school tour dedicated to non-traditional careers in the arts and entertainment, designed to show students that success can take a shape no one ever drew for them.

The philosophy is matched by a record. Through A-List Marketing & Entertainment Group, Smickle’s back-to-school programme in the west Kingston community of Tivoli Gardens reaches more than 700 students every year, from early childhood through tertiary level, and employs residents from the communities it serves.

Her annual Gift of Hope Christmas outreach, in partnership with Dolla Financial Services, brings toys, food, and essentials to families across Kingston each holiday season.

When Hurricane Melissa devastated western Jamaica, she answered with a three-phase relief effort. Phase one, with PROVEN Wealth, delivered supplies to Petersfield, Darliston, and Water Works in Westmoreland. Phase two, Joy to the West, sent her team out of Kingston before sunrise on December 24, 2025, to support young mothers at the Women’s Centre of Jamaica Foundation in Savanna-la-Mar; students at Llandilo School of Special Education; and families on Crooke Street, where a community space became a day of games, bounce houses, and supplies.

Phase three, now in development, will re-roof homes for the families hit hardest.

For all the work, Smickle is candid about how rarely she stops to acknowledge herself. “I want to say something I do not say often: I am proud of myself,” she declared. “I’m proud that I did not give up and proud that I kept believing in my vision even when others questioned it.“

She is already looking past the milestone. By 2030, she plans to expand to the United States and the Caribbean, growing both the business and the foundation that carries her mother’s name.

“Entrepreneurship is not only about building a successful company; it is about building stronger communities,” she said. “Success is measured not by personal achievements alone, but by the number of lives uplifted along the way. For the dreamers, the believers, and the ones bold enough to begin, this one is for you.”

World.title: Inquiet des usages de l’IA par les députés, le Parlement européen a une solution
World.content:
“Le Parlement n’a pas été épargné par les erreurs liées à l’IA et les contenus trompeurs générés par IA”, a observé Brando Benifei, député européen du groupe des Socialistes et démocrates qui a dirigé les travaux du Parlement sur l’AI Act, la législation phare de l’UE encadrant cette technologie. “Les députés européens doivent montrer l’exemple à mesure que les règles de transparence prévues par l’AI Act entrent en vigueur.”

Ce projet met en lumière le dilemme auquel est confronté le Parlement à mesure que l’IA générative s’intègre dans son travail. Quelque 2 100 personnes utilisent quotidiennement l’IA, soit environ 20% de l’ensemble des effectifs.

Ses dirigeants souhaitent que les responsables publics cessent de mettre des documents parlementaires sur des plateformes publiques non contrôlées, mais ils craignent également que cette technologie ne nuise à la qualité du travail législatif et n’introduise des erreurs ou des contenus trompeurs dans le processus démocratique. Ils ont soupçonné que les parlementaires et leurs assistants utilisaient déjà l’IA après une recrudescence d’amendements nécessitant une traduction, des styles de rédaction révélateurs et des références parfois fantaisistes à des lois qui n’existent pas.

Les présidents des commissions ont demandé au secrétaire général du Parlement, Alessandro Chiocchetti, d’élaborer des lignes directrices concernant l’utilisation de l’IA par les parlementaires. Celui-ci a répondu que cette question pourrait plutôt relever de la commission des Affaires constitutionnelles, qui devrait alors modifier le règlement intérieur de l’institution afin d’introduire des règles plus strictes.

Aujourd’hui, les députés européens ne sont pas tenus d’indiquer si leurs amendements, questions ou autres travaux parlementaires ont été élaborés à l’aide de l’intelligence artificielle.

Barry Andrews, président Renew de la commission du Développement, a affirmé qu’il était déjà évident que certains députés européens utilisaient l’intelligence artificielle pour rédiger des questions parlementaires, des discours et des amendements.

World.title: EU hits China’s Alibaba with €550M record fine over illegal products
World.content:
The finding that AliExpress failed to check and tackle these risks "is very dangerous for our consumers, but it’s also unfair for those companies that are complying with all our rules," Virkkunen said.

The record fine is the third one imposed under the Digital Services Act so far. It comes two months after Brussels hit rival marketplace Temu with a €200 million bill over similar breaches. “We were looking at the duration and the seriousness of these failures when deciding the size of the fine," Virkkunen said, recalling that Temu had so far only been sanctioned for failing to check its service for illegal products sold in Europe properly.

The Commission opened a probe into AliExpress in March 2024 over suspected breaches of the DSA, including also on the platform's transparency on advertising and recommender systems. Many of these suspected breaches were already settled in a series of commitments in June 2025.

In its new findings, the EU assessed that AliExpress failed to "evaluate whether it had sufficient staff to review potentially illegal products," leading to "overcharged" moderators having "only like 10 or 20 seconds to review the illegal product," a senior Commission official said in a briefing ahead of the announcement. It also failed to assess how its recommender and advertising systems "exacerbate" the spread of illegal products and relied on compliance checks that "could easily be circumvented through mis-categorization."

AliExpress has until Oct. 20 to come up with an "action plan" to address the infringements, which lasted at least until June 2025, or face additional penalties.

A spokesperson for AliExpress called the fine "disproportionate" in a statement on Monday and said the company "has been, and continues to be, firmly committed to meeting our obligations and we have invested substantial resources in risk assessment and mitigation, product safety and consumer protection."

The spokesperson added that AliExpress is "carefully reviewing the decision and considering all available options."

This article was updated to include a comment from AliExpress.

World.title: America’s reassurance mission at Farnborough
World.content:
Europe’s biggest airshow of the year is set to open this week under the specter of two wars, with the Pentagon facing doubts it can hit a trillion-dollar budget topline and if it will play nice with NATO nations increasingly confident about going it alone.

The show that spans more than five million square feet — enough to fit 78 football pitches or 1,350 Concordes stacked wing to wing — has been running since the end of World War II and will launch tens of billions of dollars worth of deals. But with the U.S. delaying arms sales and hanging onto more weapons, the feeling is in the air that American credibility — especially their ability to clarify what they want from Europe and to meet demand — is on the line here at Farnborough.

“There's no question that the primary subtext to this air show, last year's air show, I'm sure next year's air show, is going to be the geopolitical issues and the transatlantic issue in particular, and a lot of anxiety about what that means on both sides,” said a U.S. industry official. “Europe is far from a monolith. You have European countries that would absolutely like to push full on the gas to build an organic defense industrial base. You have others that are very clear they want to continue to buy American kit.”

“We still argue that we make the best stuff in the world, and everybody wants it,” added the official, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “But the Europeans are worried if they can get it.”

Scar tissue: Even as top European officials acknowledge they will need America’s help rearming, some are chafing at the Trump administration’s suggestions that the continent shouldn’t try to replace the U.S. defense industry’s role — even as the Pentagon is signaling that it is removing some U.S. forces from Europe.

“The U.S. is moving the goalpost while demanding Europe take ‘primary responsibility’ for its own defense while opposing the industrial-policy tools to do it,” said Oscar Jonsson, a specialist from the Swedish Defence University. “Most European states figured that buying American won’t reverse the trend of U.S. withdrawal, and it will only prolong an overdependence on the U.S. It’s not unlikely that there will be a compromise with some more buying American, but it’s only a slight delay to the structural shift.”

World.title: Pistorius makes fresh push for Hegseth meeting after spring setback
World.content:
The plans are still being prepared and the individual meetings depend on the minister’s final schedule.

The German defense ministry declined to comment on the plans. However, it would be Pistorius’ second attempt this year to secure a dedicated meeting with Hegseth in Washington.

The German minister abandoned the U.S. leg of a planned North America trip in May after a meeting with Hegseth could not be arranged. Pistorius went ahead with the Canadian portion of the trip, while Hegseth traveled to the Shangri-La Dialogue security conference in Singapore.

The episode was a setback for Berlin as it sought direct access to the Trump administration during a period of growing uncertainty over Washington's military role in Europe.

Pistorius and Hegseth have met before. Most recently, both were at the NATO Summit in Ankara. And during a formal Pentagon visit in July 2025, the two discussed the future of U.S. forces in Europe and Germany's interest in the American Typhon long-range missile system as well as Tomahawk missiles.

Those questions have only become more pressing. Hegseth announced in June a six-month review of U.S. troop deployments in Europe, while Washington has already reduced some of the military capabilities it makes available to NATO. Pistorius has warned that any American withdrawal must be coordinated with European allies to avoid dangerous gaps in the alliance’s defenses.

World.title: Burnham fires Starmer allies as he becomes UK PM — live updates
World.content:
Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham gives his first speech in front of No. 10 Downing St. in central London on July 20, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images

The country’s sixth prime minister in a decade is getting going — picking his cabinet, and calling Donald Trump. Follow along live.

LONDON — Britain got (another) new prime minister Monday: Andy Burnham.

The former mayor of Greater Manchester — who succeeded Keir Starmer as leader of the U.K.’s governing Labour Party last week — will shortly start naming his top team after King Charles III asked him to form a government. He has already fired key allies of his predecessor Keir Starmer, including top finance minister Rachel Reeves.

Burnham is Britain’s sixth prime minister in the past decade alone, and his appointment comes as the governing Labour Party gambles that another change at the top will turn around a polling deficit at the hands of right-wing populist Nigel Farage.

In his first speech in the job — delivered without notes or the customary lectern that previous new prime ministers have used — Burnham promised action on the cost of living within days, and a 10-year plan for government to follow later in the year.

He said he would immediately order officials to work to end homelessness in the U.K. — and he’s held his first call with U.S. President Donald Trump.

Now expect a flurry of announcements through the day on Burnham’s picks for the Cabinet. Follow the POLITICO team below for the latest — and brush up on Burnham with these primers:

World.title: The 59th PM: What lies ahead for Burnham
World.content:
The bloodless coup reaches its climax today as Andy Burnham is set to become the 59th prime minister of the United Kingdom – but does a new face mark a new era of British politics?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy dissect the choreography of the handover, preview Burnham’s first words as PM and analyse the key cabinet appointments that will reveal the shape of his government.

Will anything really change?

The duo also consider how a small cosmetic change could signal a new way in which Andy Burnham wants to operate.

Plus, with little policy on the table so far, Sam and Anne assess the early indicators and direction of strategy and how it will impact the work of his incoming chancellor.

World.title: Brussels proposes easing methane penalties after heavy lobbying from industry
World.content:
The European Commission has proposed waiving penalties linked to the bloc's methane rules for three years.

 

Industry and top liquefied natural gas (LNG) exporters have been pressuring Brussels over its burdensome reporting requirements, which they said could affect exports to the European Union.

EU member states adopted methane rules in May 2024, introducing the bloc’s first framework for measuring, reporting and verifying methane emissions in the energy sector as part of efforts to curb one of the most potent greenhouse gases. Failure to honor such requests would incur penalties, which would start applying in 2027.

But on Monday, the Commission recommended exempting business operators from full compliance.

The much-anticipated recommendations come after months of lobbying from the United States, Qatar, Algeria and Nigeria, who warned the EU executive that its rules would endanger the EU's security of supply at a time when the bloc is struggling to offset losses from the Middle East – a claim hotly contested by environmentalists.

Green organisations warned that broad discretion to waive penalties could weaken one of the world's most ambitious efforts to curb emissions of methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent in the short term than carbon dioxide.

"A three-year sanction holiday, triggered by exaggerated and unsubstantiated security of supply concerns raised by industry, risks giving a free pass to methane-intensive gas imports – notably from the US," said Esther Bollendorff, fossil free program manager at Climate Action Network Europe.

Bollendorff argued that the recommendations "should not deter member states from implementing robust penalty systems", arguing that such actions are "essential to ensuring that companies pay the price for their pollution".

"These recommendations should be reviewed well before the suggested 2028 timeline, to suspend their application as soon as possible," Bollendorff added.

Contractual law for regulatory certainty

In the four-page recommendation, Brussels also instructs importers how to write contracts that will allow them to comply with the rules.

The recommendations don't create new legal obligations, but they provide optional model contract clauses that energy importers can use to comply with the methane rules – a response business operators' calls for regulatory certainty.

"The optional model clauses are intended to promote fair, transparent and sustainable contractual practices, to provide a framework for the adjustment of contractual terms, to support compliance (...) and to foster reliable supply of crude oil, natural gas, LNG or coal to the Union," the Commission's recommendations say.

Industry groups say the Commission has acknowledged flaws in the methane rules that could threaten Europe's energy security, but argue its proposed non-binding guidance falls short.

Related US Democrats urge Brussels to stick to methane rules

"The Commission persists in wanting to fix them through non-binding guidance, which cannot deliver the uniform legal certainty Europe needs. Only targeted amendments, as called for by Member States and industry, can," a spokesperson from the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers told Euronews.

With fewer than six months before key provisions take effect, businesses warn that delays are already affecting commercial decisions and supply contracts. They urge the EU to fast-track targeted amendments that maintain methane reduction goals while safeguarding the EU's security of supply, competitiveness and consumers from higher costs.

Maas Goote, international lawyer and former EU lead negotiator at UN climate talks, welcomed the Commission's "wise approach" by "offering pragmatic solutions for implementation issues and strengthening the EU methane regime step-by-step".

"In doing so, it is important that the integrity of the Regulation remains intact,” Goote noted. "The upward trend of methane emissions worldwide shows that voluntary approaches are not delivering results. We need strong regulatory frameworks to drive down methane emissions, with the EU methane regulation as a strong and critical piece."

World.title: Rare 48C heatwave forces Uzbekistan to adapt to extreme temperatures
World.content:
An intense heatwave disrupted daily life across Uzbekistan, prompting authorities to take urgent measures to protect the public as temperatures reached 42C–45C across much of the country.

 

Temperatures climbed to 46C–48C in southern and desert regions, putting pressure on public services and forcing residents to adapt their daily routines.

Fire and rescue teams maintained round-the-clock duty near markets, shopping centres and other crowded locations to prevent fires and respond rapidly to emergencies.

Emergency crews also used fire and rescue vehicles to spray water for children in residential neighbourhoods during the hottest part of the day.

“For several days, the Ministry of Emergency Situations has been organising these activities for children in residential areas,” said Murat Sadykov, head of the ministry’s Information Service.

“Fire and rescue vehicles visit areas where children have gathered and spray them with water. During the peak of the summer heat, this helps them cool down and also lifts their spirits.”

40 degrees in the middle of the day Euronews

The Ministry of Emergency Situations intensified public information campaigns, advising residents on how to protect themselves from extreme temperatures.

“We are carrying out extensive awareness campaigns and informing people about important recommendations on how to protect themselves from the heat and its consequences,” Sadykov said.

“We urge people to drink as much water as possible and to wear light-coloured, preferably white, cotton clothing.”

The Tashkent city administration increased water spraying on central and major roads and stepped up watering of trees and lawns.

Fountains across the capital were also switched to continuous operation as authorities sought to reduce the impact of the prolonged heat in public spaces.

'You can really feel the difference'

Residents and visitors alike were surprised by the sudden spike in temperature, which is highly unusual for Uzbekistan at this time of the year.

“We came here for a textile exhibition and were not expecting such extreme heat,” Altyn Bakiyeva, a visitor from Bishkek in neighbouring Kyrgyzstan, told Euronews.

“It is also very hot in our country, but it is a few degrees hotter here and you can really feel the difference," Bakiyeva said.

"We try to cope by using air-conditioned taxis, and fortunately our hotel also has air conditioning. Cold water is the only thing that helps.”

Fountains keep running continuously Euronews

Tashkent resident Odinakhon Akramova said families were changing their eating habits and drinking more water.

“We drink a lot of water. We put watermelons and melons in the refrigerator and eat them when they are cold. We mainly eat fruit and prepare only small amounts of cooked food," Akramova said.

The measures formed part of a broader response involving municipal services, transport operators, education authorities and emergency teams.

Emergency services step up prevention efforts

Public transport operators and regional authorities also introduced measures intended to protect infrastructure and reduce safety risks.

In Tashkent, trains on above-ground sections of the metro temporarily operated at 40 kilometres per hour instead of the usual 60 kilometres per hour.

Tashkent Metro JSC said the restriction was introduced because rail temperatures on elevated sections had exceeded the standard limit of 55C. The reduced speed remained in force until 6 pm each day.

In the southern Surkhandarya Region, the movement of heavy vehicles was restricted on some roads between 10 am and 7 pm local time.

Regional authorities said road surfaces could reach temperatures of 70C–80C, weakening the asphalt and increasing the risk of damage from heavy trucks.

Authorities also temporarily closed kindergartens in some of the areas most affected by the heat.

In Karakalpakstan, preschool facilities in Nukus and eight districts were closed following the sharp rise in temperatures, according to the Ministry of Preschool and School Education.

All state-run kindergartens in the Khorezm Region were also closed from last Tuesday to Friday, while restrictions were introduced in several districts of the Navoi Region.

The extreme conditions were expected to ease gradually later this week.

World.title: People’s photos are helping scientists record marine life in real-time in the Canary Islands
World.content:
With more than 85,000 recorded and validated sightings in the waters of the so-called ‘Lucky Islands’ or Macaronesia, scientists from the RedPROMAR project have recorded more than 5,000 species of living organisms in this part of the North Atlantic.

 

Dennis Rabeling, a diving instructor at Euro-Divers Lanzarote, is one of its main contributors. He dives every day and uploads thousands of photos of marine flora and fauna to the website of this European project, which is co-funded by the Government of the Canary Islands. He has contributed to the discovery of three species previously unknown in the Canary Islands, one of which is named after him: Gibberula Dennisi. “With RedPROMAR, if you upload your photos, you become another pair of eyes on the water. In this way, scientists can identify new species that we did not previously know lived here. Today, during a thirty-minute dive, we saw around twenty or thirty species, perhaps even more," he explains.

Through this project, ocean culture is brought into the classroom, and the classroom is brought closer to the sea. This year, secondary school pupils from Juan Francisco Rodríguez García’s class at IES Yaiza have studied how human activities affect the marine environment, recorded a podcast on tropicalisation and its consequences, and undertaken a field trip to Órzola, in the north of Lanzarote, to learn ‘in situ’ which species live in the sea and how RedPROMAR works.

“We’ve taught them about a tool which allows any member of the public, including them, to take a photo of a particular species and geotag it using the same app, in order to provide better scientific data and contribute to scientific research” Juan Francisco Rodríguez García Environmental educator and teacher, IES Yaiza

An experience their pupils will never forget. Aroa says, “I didn’t even know most of the species. I hadn’t heard those names before at all. Take the manatee, for example. When an animal tries to bother it, it releases a kind of purple ink to scare it away. It’s really amazing."

The total budget for the project is just under two million euros, of which 85% has been funded by the European Cohesion Policy and the remaining 15% by the Canary Islands Government.

The pieces of the photo jigsaw speak

This project began in the Canary Islands and has since expanded its scope to Cape Verde, Madeira and the Azores. Each geotagged photo is checked by a team of experts. Marc Martín Sola, a marine biologist at Gesplan and a technician with RedPROMAR, says that “citizen science data is like a jigsaw puzzle, in which observers provide us with small pieces that, taken individually, may not make sense”, but when put together, they are valuable to the scientific community and to the authorities.

“By putting all these pieces together, we can see things that we wouldn’t be able to see individually; for example, introduced species or protected species, and we can better assess a species’ distribution or breeding season” Marc Martín Sola Marine biologist at Gesplan and technician with RedPROMAR

The platform also serves as an early-warning system for the arrival of alien species and the proliferation of species linked to human activity or climate change. “There are specific times when we receive a lot of reports, a lot of sightings of a particular species, and this usually coincides with ‘arribazones’ (washed ashore) – the mass arrival of organisms, whether alive or dead, on the coast,” explains Marc. “In 2024, we had more than a hundred sightings in just a few months. "Citizen science enables us to detect and record these sudden surges that might otherwise go unnoticed by the scientific community and thus keep a record of when and where they have occurred," he concludes.

World.title: Yemen’s Houthis threaten Bab el-Mandeb closure in embargo on Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthis on Monday announced they are imposing a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia in retaliation for a blockade on Yemen and a recent attack on Sanaa International Airport, threatening another vital waterway for global shipping and raising fears of renewed conflict.

 

A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said in a video statement that the maritime ban against Saudi Arabia will be effective immediately, describing it as an "equation of 'an eye for an eye.'"

The Houthis did not specify how the embargo would be enforced, but the deputy head of the Houthi media office, Nasruddin Amer, said on X that the Bab el-Mandeb strait will be closed in response to what he called Saudi Arabia's "unjust blockade on Yemenis for over 10 years."

Bab el-Mandeb, at the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula — whose name means "Gate of Tears" in Arabic — is the gateway to the Red Sea through which around 12% of the world's trade usually passes. A fourth of global container trade transits through the 32-kilometre-wide strait to and from the Suez Canal.

A closure would force vessels to take the much longer route around the Cape of Good Hope, adding two to three weeks to journeys between Asia and Europe and sharply increasing shipping costs.

The Houthis — formally known as Ansar Allah — earlier demonstrated their ability to disrupt shipping there when they targeted ships for months over the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, with over 100 vessels attacked.

Many major shipping companies suspended transits through the Red Sea during the campaign, while the US and several allies launched a multinational naval mission to protect commercial shipping.

It is unclear whether the Houthis will resume that level of attack against neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

There was no immediate response from Saudi Arabia. The kingdom already faced pressure as it uses its East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under a blockade Tehran imposed shortly after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February in the opening salvo of the war.

Saudi Arabia has been sending millions of barrels of crude oil a day through the pipeline.

'Respond to blockade with a blockade'

Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the rebels seized the capital, Sana'a, and much of northern Yemen and forced the government into exile. A truce was reached in 2022.

That truce has been threatened in recent days after the Houthis said the Saudis struck the Sana'a airport in an attempt to affect a flight carrying Houthi leaders back from Iran, where they attended the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The plane landed safely at another airport.

The Houthis then launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia's Abha International Airport in the most significant confrontation in years.

By allowing a direct international flight to land without the approval of the Saudi-led coalition, the Houthis sought to establish a new reality in which they could independently make decisions over Yemen's airspace.

The coalition has long maintained control over access to Yemen's airspace and ports as part of measures it says are intended to prevent weapons from reaching the Houthis, while the rebels argue the restrictions amount to collective punishment.

"We affirm the right of our great people to respond to the blockade with a blockade," Saree emphasised on Monday, adding that Houthis are prepared to confront "any foolish act committed by the reckless Saudi enemy ... with a comprehensive and decisive escalation."

The Houthis are a crucial part of Iran's so-called "Axis of Resistance," which also includes Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq.

The rebels have had a large stockpile of drones, but several Houthi members previously said that the supply was running low after their attacks during the Israel-Hamas war.

The Iran war has further impeded the flow of weapons, said the members, who at the time spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to talk to the media.

The US and Israel responded to the Houthis' earlier attacks on shipping with a punishing air campaign across Houthi-held areas in Yemen until a deal was reached that saw the rebels stop their assaults.

The previous Houthi campaign contributed to higher freight rates, longer delivery times and renewed concerns over supply chains already strained by wars in Europe and the Middle East.

World.title: From 'Following' to 'The Odyssey': All Christopher Nolan movies ranked from weakest to strongest
World.content:
From sci-fi thrillers to historical dramas via layered mysteries and three hugely successful Batman films, few directors inspire as much devotion as Christopher Nolan.

 

You know the fans we're talking about. The Nolanites who gush about every film and batter away recurring criticism of style-over-substance, emotional coldness, or the fact that he'd do well to forgo non-chronological narrative tampering in order to prioritise three-dimensional female characters that aren't just there to be dead wives.

Then there are those who recognise these pitfalls but can't deny that the Oscar winner continues to wow with an eclectic filmography featuring reoccurring motifs, arresting visual flourishes, and an ability to command top-notch talent both in front and behind the camera.

Whichever camp you're in, and whatever you may think of his box-office dominating latest, The Odyssey, Euronews Culture looks back and re-assesses all of the director's movies from weakest to strongest.

13) Following (1998)

Following Momentum Pictures

Every director has to start somewhere, and for then-28-year-old Christopher Nolan it was a 70-minute black-and-white drama about an obsessive writer. The 'Young Man' (Jeremy Theobald) follows strangers around London for inspiration and gets in over his head when he breaks his one rule: never follow the same person twice. This cerebral neo-noir is striking due to its Hitchcockian effectiveness, and features some of Nolan's treasured themes - principally topics of obsession and identity. Following is a decent entry point into Nolan's world and it's impressive to watch it with his second film (Memento) in mind to appreciate quite how the director evolved in leaps and bounds. Beyond that perspective and his debut being a micro-budget curio in his filmography (it was reportedly made for $6000), Following does remain a promising, if sluggish, character study.

12) Tenet (2020)

Tenet Warner Bros. Pictures

You can't accuse Tenet of not being ambitious. It's a high-concept and technically impressive espionage story which trusts the audience to keep up with time inversion and palindromic shenanigans. But it's the movie which showed that Nolan's reach exceeded his grasp. John David Washington plays a secret agent (eyerollingly dubbed “The Protagonist”) trying to prevent a war between the present and the future. It's thrilling in theory but baffling in execution. Tenet gets increasingly frustrating when it becomes a checklist of Nolan's most irritating foibles: pseudo-profundity lost in clumsy dialogue, underwritten female characters, oppressive sound mixing, and stunning style over pretentious substance. Even if you do embrace the advice given by a Tenet scientist ("Don't try to understand it, feel it"), you'll still be confronted with an emotionally cold effort which is convinced it's a lot cleverer than it actually is.

11) Insomnia (2002)

Insomnia Warner Bros. Pictures

Nolan's third film may not one of his most memorable, but it's certainly underappreciated. Insomnia is a remake of Erik Skjoldbjærg’s 1997 thriller starring Stellan Skarsgård, and follows a veteran detective (Al Pacino) who teams up with a small-town investigator (Hilary Swank) to solve a Laura Palmer-reminiscent murder in a remote part of Alaska. Remote and bathed in perpetual sunlight. It’s a captivating detective drama, and what it lacks in ambitious scope it makes up for in upended tropes, an audaciously bleak ending, as well as a stellar performance from Robin Williams playing against type. Granted, Insomnia feels like it was a studio-mandated assignment for Nolan (who delivered his first film for Warner Bros.), but as far as psychological thrillers go, it deserves your time of day.

10) The Dark Knight Rises (2012)

The Dark Knight Rises Warner Bros. Pictures

It's a shame that Christopher Nolan's Dark Knight Trilogy ended with a bit of a whimper with The Dark Knight Rises. Sure, Tom Hardy was great as Bane and Anne Hathaway impressed as Catwoman, but in making the story's scope wider (Charles Dickens' "A Tale of Two Cities" was a reference point for Nolan), something got lost along the way. The script isn't as tight, the plot holes are glaring, and some of the acting is questionable... Quite how that was the take chosen for Miranda Tate (Marion Cotillard)'s death, we'll never know... Nothing here reaches the same heights as Batman Begins or The Dark Knight. Granted, the latter was a tricky act to follow (more on that later), but it's undeniable that this closing chapter settles for satisfactory.

9) Dunkirk (2017)

Dunkirk Warner Bros. Pictures

From the very first shot, Dunkirk announces itself as something special. And it is: an astonishingly well-made World War II film that is split between land, sea and air. All three parts are intercut together while maintaining their individual pace. A week for land; a day for sea; an hour for air. By segmenting his depiction of the Dunkirk evacuation into these timelines and making them share a common theme (survival), Nolan delivers a technically accomplished experience whose visuals take precedent over traditional narrative storytelling. While it's a technical marvel which throws you into the action, Dunkirk does suffer from keeping the audience at an emotional distance when it comes to the many protagonists. As for the ending, some shots are jaw-dropping but their impact is dented by a clichéd ending featuring Commander Bolton (Kenneth Branagh) saying he's stayng "for the French." Groan.

8) Interstellar (2014)

Interstellar Warner Bros. Pictures

Interstellar is Christopher Nolan aiming to make this generation's 2001: A Space Odyssey, only with a more emotional core. By charting how an astronaut (Matthew McConaughey) leaves behind his children (not that you'd know, as most of the focus is on his daughter Murph) in a quest to save humanity by finding a new world to replace a dying Earth, Nolan attempts to prove some of his detractors wrong. He can put aside the coldly clinical and is capable of embracing feelings. For much of the runtime, the self-serious theoretical astrophysics blend well with the human drama, and some sequences are jaw-dislocatingly good. The "wave planet" and its time distortion is a particular highlight. The snag is that while Interstellar is never not awe-inspiring, thanks in large part to Hoyte van Hoytema's cinematography, the dialogue is distractingly on-the-nose and the final act fumbles the father-daughter story when it all goes M. Night Shyamalan in a five-dimensional space bookshelf. It's an imperfect film - made worse by countless film bros insisting that you the reason you don't love it more is because you don't understand it. But there's no denying that ambitious sci-fi never looked this spectacular.

7) The Odyssey (2026)

The Odyssey Universal Pictures

You've resurrected Batman, performed a dream heist (Inception), gone into outer-space and finally won several Oscars for your three-hour biopic about the birth of the atomic bomb... What do you do next? Embrace your inner Kubrick by fearing no scale nor scope and adapt the borderline unadaptable oldest known work of literature. As if that wasn't enough, you shoot it all in IMAX for a world first. Nolan’s take on Homer's epic is without a doubt his most ambitious undertaking, and there's so much to admire about this monumental technical achievement. Also worth singling out is his departure from the traditional Homeric world, preferring a tale in which the supernatural elements are dialled back to make way for a modernist reading of Odysseus' psyche. However, the filmmaker's proclivity for non-linear plot structures proves to be a thorn in his side. The Odyssey is often crippled by clumsy editing choices and pacing issues in its first half, and he never spends enough time on the dangerous adventures to make thrills truly register. Once it does coalesce into something more focused in the final act, you'll have felt awe but not much in the way of character-driven emotion. Even if it isn't the flat-out masterpiece many are hailing, there's no denying that no one could have accomplished something so bold.

6) Oppenheimer (2023)

Oppenheimer Universal Pictures

You’ve got to hand it to Oppenheimer - a three-hour biopic about a bunch of scientists, generals and lawmen talking to each other became 2023’s most unlikely blockbuster pairing with Barbie. It had no right being as gripping as it was. Based on Kai Bird and Martin J Sherwin’s non-fiction book "American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer", Nolan’s chronologically skewed epic gives spectators an exhaustive look at the rise and fall of the theoretical physicist who oversaw the Manhattan Project and introduced nuclear weapons to humanity. It's an American tragedy which benefits from the talents of an all-star cast led by Cillian Murphy and his note-perfect performance. Themes of guilt hit hard; the pace feels more deliberate compared to The Odyssey; and Ludwig Göransson's score is still his crowning achievement. One sizeable issue remains: Nolan still can’t write female roles – which is glaring here considering Oppenheimer features two complex women played by the immensely talented Emily Blunt and Florence Pugh.

5) Batman Begins (2005)

Batman Begins Warner Bros. Pictures

The Batman franchise was dead and buried after 1997’s Batman & Robin, and it took Christopher Nolan to revive the Caped Crusader for a new generation of cinemagoers. Starting with the very origins of Bruce Wayne before he donned the cowl, Nolan approached this superhero story much like he did The Odyssey: out with the myth and in with the character-driven story of a traumatised man. His hyper-realistic take on the Bat dispelled memories of Burton’s gothic treatment and Schumacher’s campy kitsch, and reinvented the franchise by showing that a grown-up Dark Knight was possible. Kudos to Christian Bale for understanding the assignment and making the parallels and conflicts between Bruce Wayne and Bats so engaging. It was the thrilling start of something special – but we’ll get to that in a bit.

4) Inception (2010)

Inception Warner Bros. Pictures

From this point in the ranking, there are nothing but triumphs. But because decisions have to be made, it's 2010's Inception which narrowly misses the podium. Following Leonardo DiCaprio as a grief-stricken widower who specializes in a form of corporate espionage involving the theft of information from a mark’s subconscious, Inception is one of the most original blockbusters of the 21st century. Getting the balance just right between cerebral and thrilling, Nolan proved that an A-list populated Hollywood action caper could be Bond-indebted and audaciously mind-melting. Moreover, the director gave the audience credit by trusting them to keep up during the matryoshkadream ride. Beyond the now parodied Hans Zimmer score and its blaring horns, Inception remains the bar to clear when it comes to films that both dazzle and challenge.

3) Memento (2000)

Memento Newmarket

Nolan's second film is the one that put him on the map as a singular talent to watch. His sophomore effort is an engrossing and twisty noir about a man (Guy Pierce) unable to create short-term memories. As if that wasn't tough enough to deal with, our hero is trying to solve his wife's murder. Before Inception upped the stakes in terms of scope, Memento showed that Nolan was capable of making thrilling and challenging films which didn't talk down to audiences. Since its release, there have been misguided corners of the internet keen to dismiss Memento as "gimmicky". It's anything but. Beyond the chronological momentum of the monochrome scenes and the backward trajectory of the colour frames, Nolan takes the time to explore themes of grief, guilt and self-deception within a fractured mind. His film still stands as a groundbreaking mystery thriller that proves the director is at his nonlinear best when he keeps a tight grip on the narrative and never forgoes psychological depth for structural flourishes.

2) The Dark Knight (2008)

The Dark Knight Warner Bros. Pictures

After Batman Begins, Nolan originally had no plans to return to Gotham. Everyone was glad he did, as The Dark Knight still stands to this day as one of the – if not the – greatest comic book / superhero movie ever made. Continuing his deconstruction the Batman myth, Nolan saw fit to shake things up and introduce the franchise's most beloved antagonist: The Joker. Despite initial bellyaching from fans that Heath Ledger was miscast as the Clown Prince of Crime, the latter delivered an Oscar-winning performance that was elevated to iconic following the actor's untimely death. Beyond the performances and thrills, The Dark Knight is an expansive and thematically rich blockbuster which continues to divide cinemalovers. Which is the superior middle instalment: The Empire Strikes Back or The Dark Knight ?

1) The Prestige (2006)

The Prestige Warner Bros. Pictures

Based on Christopher Priest’s novel about dueling turn-of-the-century magicians - the charismatic Robert Angier (Hugh Jackman) and the technically skilled Alfred Borden (Christian Bale) - The Prestige didn't make much of a splash when it came out. Turning 20 this year, it takes the top spot. Structured in three fiendishly orchestrated parts mirroring (and adopting) the stages of a magic trick (The Pledge / The Turn / The Prestige), this is Nolan at his most disciplined when it comes to his time-based perspective shifts. The structure directly complements the narrative, making it a necessary formal trick. The Prestige is also Nolan at his most diligent when it comes to character development, and the way he explores themes of obsession and sacrifice hit home. Moreover, Nolan makes his film enticingly metatextual, a layered slight of hand that becomes not only about two ego-driven characters chasing the perfect illusion but about the medium of cinema itself. Fans may argue that The Odyssey is Nolan's most awe-inspiring feat, but this may just be about the scale and... whisper it... recency bias. They should consider The Prestige as the film which continues to leave spectactors open-mouthed. The twists stun upon first viewing; its layers deepen with repeated watches; and it continues to impress 20 years later. “You don’t really want to know the secret; you want to be fooled.” Too true. The Prestige is not only the greatest film ever made about magic, but Nolan's finest achievement to date.

The Odyssey is out in cinemas now.
